speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: At the suspension of the debate the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands had seven minutes remaining.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to complete my remarks on this bill and to reinforce my opposition to this project, the fixed link in the Northumberland Strait.
My principal concern is the protection of the marine environment in the Northumberland Strait. This bridge will be constructed in the midst of a habitat which supports a $100 million a year fishery providing lobsters to North America and the world. It would also pass through one of the area's largest known scallop beds.
The bridge also threatens the physical and social environment of the island and the earning capacity of many diverse individuals and communities, including fishermen, ferry workers, retailers, food processors and tourist operators.
In 1988, the federal government promised that no bridge would ever be built without a full environmental assessment of the specific bridge design. That was its response to a number of concerns about a generic bridge design. Now, it seems to be pretending that an environ-

February 22, 1993

mental management plan, a short, vague description of construction monitoring, is an environmental assessment. So much for the 1988 promise. So much for Canada's environmental credibility.
I want to go back to the federal environment assessment review process. When the federal government is involved in a major project which could affect the environment, the activity must undergo an environmental assessment and review process.
The Prince Edward Island bridge project was deemed to be such a project and the federal Environmental Assessment Review Office convened an independent six-member panel on April 28, 1989. Its mandate was to conduct a public review of three concept proposals for a bridge. It was never explained why a tunnel or improved feriy service were not considered as part of the publicly financed review.
The panel was asked to examine the environmental and socioeconomic effects of an imaginary bridge crossing without blueprints or actual design specifications. It was also asked to determine the possible effect of the construction operation and maintenance of the project and its associated facilities.
Public hearings were held in the three maritime provinces between March 12 and March 30, 1990. Over 1,500 people attended the 21 sessions. The intensity of public participation in the hearings gave credibility to a process that islanders initially viewed with some skepticism.
After that extensive public discussion as well as in depth technical and bureaucratic consultations, the FEARO panel released its final report in August, 1990. The panel unanimously rejected the generic concept of the bridge presented to it by Public Works. Its rejection was based on numerous significant concerns.
Let us understand what has happened. There was an environmental assessment of a generic bridge concept.
The panel recommended that the bridge project not proceed because of the following reasons: The potential impacts on marine ecosystems and agricultural microclimates arising from delayed spring ice-out; the risk of
Government Orders
damage to near shore spawning grounds; the limited knowledge of the Northumberland Strait ecosystem making it difficult to predict impacts, monitor impacts, mitigate impacts and determine appropriate compensation to fishermen; incompatibility of the project with sustainable development; inadequate consideration of cumulative impacts; difficulties in finding socially acceptable solutions for displaced ferry workers and fishermen; inadequate consideration of the environmental and ecological impacts of the island on the predicted type of tourism and growth; and the need to resolve numerous land use issues in Prince Edward Island.
In conclusion the panel has noted there is a need for improved transportation service between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. After careful consideration, the panel concludes that the risk of harmful effects of the proposed bridge concept is unacceptable. The panel recommends therefore that the project not proceed.
What has this government done now? It has put forward an ice panel which refutes what the FEARO panel recommended. It is now trying to put forward and push this specific bridge concept ahead without environmental assessment. It is no wonder the people of Canada are cynical about the way this government operates.
I would also like to point out that there are considerations other than environmental. A Financial Post article of February 17 states:
The federal government has not done the math to support building a bridge to Prince Edward Island.
The September 1992 report by Halifax-based Gardner Pinfold Consulting Economists says a key 1987 economic feasibility assessment of a fixed crossing has several flaws.
If economic viability is an important criterion for proceeding with the project, then it would be advisable to conduct a more rigorous analysis.
In conclusion, this bridge concept is not environmentally sound nor economically sound. It should be shelved until a full environmental impact assessment has been done on the particular project. Anything less is a repudiation of this government's own environmental assessment review process. It puts into doubt the whole environmental assessment review process put forward by this government.
I urge the House not to support Bill C-110.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-110 is the enabling legislation for a major infrastructure project that not only is immense in scale, but is also unique in its approach. This project is going to bring many benefits to the people of the maritimes, the Atlantic region. All provinces in the Atlantic region will benefit, but Prince Edward Island will in particular.
It is not just the people of the maritimes who will benefit. Taxpayers generally will benefit from this. What is not commonly understood across Canada is that it is a constitutional requirement that the federal government provide ongoing subsidy or support for the people of Prince Edward Island to maintain the service between the mainland and the island.
This is something that constitutionally will never cease as long as the ferry service continues. However, if the project proceeds that this legislation is dealing with, we have a situation where the ongoing cost of the ferry service will be maintained as a subsidy for 35 years. At that point in time the subsidy ceases.
Instead of the situation where for time immemorial the taxpayers of Canada will be required to maintain the ferry link between the mainland and Prince Edward Island it will in fact be fulfilled with the fixed link. There is another thing that is quite unique about this project that should be of interest to all taxpayers across Canada. It is not going to be funded in this case by the taxpayers of Canada. When they think of these major projects, they immediately perceive huge tax dollars being demanded of them. In fact, the tax dollars to support this will be those that are equivalent to what would have been paid out in the ferry service over the next 35 years.
This project will be funded, built and operated by three enterprises for the next 35 years. If we proceed successfully with this, there will be many people watching to see if this may be a framework for other major infrastructure programs. It is not just the taxpayers of Canada who will benefit. The users of the existing ferry service and the new fixed link will also benefit from it.
Something that is not commonly understood about this project is that the toll charges that will be paid by people who cross the link from the mainland to the island or vice versa will be feed so that they cannot increase to anything greater than three quarters of the inflation
factor. This means that generations to come in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick will benefit from lower rates than they would otherwise experience. To put this in perspective, if over the last decade we had had an agreement that the ferry tolls could not increase by more than three quarters of the inflation rate then the current ferry rates would have increased by less than one third of what they actually increased. It is of significant benefit to those people who are habitual users of the service.
There are other economic benefits, those that will be returned primarily to those in the maritimes. I will refer to it as the Northumberland Strait one-two punch. Punch No. 1 is that construction of this massive project will create jobs and business opportunities starting immediately and continuing through the next four or five years.
Punch No. 2 will be that in the longer term, after the link is completed, it will enhance the province's growing tourism industry and result in cost efficiencies for agriculture and many other enterprises. Construction itself is expected to generate from 3,500 to 4,000 person years of employment over the next five years.
One condition stressed by Prince Edward Island and other Atlantic provinces was that maximum employment opportunities should and would accrue to the region as the project proceeds.
It is estimated that 95 per cent of the jobs will be supplied from within Canada and over 80 per cent of those jobs are expected to accrue to the Atlantic provinces. This will have a phenomenal impact on an area of Canada that is habitually hard-pressed and deserves this improved situation. For instance, it is estimated that the unemployment rate in Prince Edward Island will decrease by over 1.3 per cent, directly attributed to the fixed link. In all, the construction of the bridge will result in a direct expenditure of about $850 million. When the effects of respending that normally take place are figured into the economy of the island, the project will represent a stimulus to the Canadian economy in the order of $1.3 billion. There will be tremendous opportunities for businesses, not only in Prince Edward Island but in New Brunswick and, in fact, across the country. I think the principal beneficiaries, as I mentioned earlier, are going to be in the maritimes.
February 22, 1993

The selected bridge design means that almost 95 per cent of the construction materials and related services can be supplied from within Canada. Even more important to the people in the maritimes is that they expect 80 per cent of it can be provided by the local suppliers. That means that opportunities will be created for a range of products and services, including supplying cement, the aggregates of the steel, selling and leasing heavy equipment, fabricating and finishing reinforcing steel, the construction of roads leading to and from the fixed link and a whole variety of other services. Many of these services are ideal for smaller local-based companies.
The immediate response from Prince Edward Island in particular has been extremely positive. By the end of January, nearly 400 Prince Edward Island businesses had expressed interest in participating and most of them have shown that interest through the Prince Edward Island Business Development Agency.
A number of firms have already directly contacted the developer as well and the response there has also been positive.
One of the key requirements for the project is that the developer maximize the use of Atlantic Canada suppliers. In fact, SCI is currently preparing an industrial benefits plan which must be submitted to and approved by the federal government before the final contracts are assigned.
There is no doubt that this bridge construction will generate substantial immediate economic benefits for all of the maritime provinces and in fact for Canada. However, I would be remiss if we did not look further down the road. What are the long-term benefits that we see? When the bridge is in operation, there will be benefits and they will be substantial. The bridge will significantly reduce the amount of time taken to transport vehicles, passengers and goods between the two provinces. Crossing time will go from a current average of over one and a half hours to the neighbourhood of 15 minutes for crossing. This will provide an extremely important benefit to all of the users.
A factor of this crossing that I had not thought of until it was pointed out to me is that there is a very significant energy saving from the link. The energy consumption will be reduced to less than one-sixth of the amount that
Government Orders
would be required if the ferries were still in operation. Of course many other sectors of the Prince Edward Island economy will be affected, in particular tourism.
Tourism is the province's second largest industry. It is expected to grow as a result of the relative ease of access. The bridge itself will become, like so many other major projects that have been built in North America, a destination. Tourists will come to see and to cross the bridge. This will draw visitors not just from Canada but from around the world.
Other major beneficiaries will be those industries that transport their goods from the island. Agriculture, fisheries and all the associated processing facilities will benefit by way of cost reductions, greater efficiency and, very important, improved reliability of delivery.
The Prince Edward Island trucking industry has gone on record with its forecast that it expects to save in the order of $10 million annually as a direct result of the bridge's construction.
There is no question that the economic arguments for proceeding with the link are strong and compelling. It represents a project that at absolute minimum cost to the taxpayer will bring both short and long-term benefits and hope for the renewal of the citizens of Canada's smallest province.
To be sure there are those islanders who oppose the project, fearing that the bridge will somehow change the province's way of life and its unique character. Similar concerns were expressed by the people of Cape Breton prior to the building of the Canso Causeway. Yet this region has seen no diminution of its distinctive character in the years since. Its tourism and other industries have clearly benefited.
The bridge will be a change to Prince Edward Island for sure, but my expectation is that it will be a change for the better.
I believe future generations of Prince Edward Island citizens will have reason to thank those who had the foresight and determination to press ahead with this great engineering undertaking.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the parliamentary secretary.

February 22, 1993
Government Orders
I know he was performing his function in his usual capable way and also that his riding is in British Columbia, which is on the other side of the continent. I listened with interest to many of his statements.
First, I would like to ask him a question about some of the concerns. In P.E.I. business is basically in favour of this move. The public has been divided. The referendum results were 60-40 in favour of a link, although not necessarily a bridge.
Let us look at the figures, which really give me concern. How can the parliamentary secretary stand there and say that the taxpayer is not going to be involved? The computed annual subsidy, which has been down to about $21 million a year, is estimated by Marine Atlantic to be $29 million over the 35-year period. Yet under this bill the Government of Canada is going to pay $42 million a year for that 35-year period. With the $29 million a year subsidy over 35 years we get a total subsidy of $1.05 billion. With the $42 million annual subsidy over a 35-year period we get a figure of $1.47 billion.
How can the parliamentary secretary and the government say that the Canadian taxpayer is not going to help the financing of this project? Why does the hon. parliamentary secretary keep saying, as the minister did when he opened the debate on this bill, that the cost of the project is going to be $800 million or $850 million? Those questions come first.
Second, I know the parliamentary secretary will be most aware, in view of recent news reports, of the Lions Gate Bridge in British Columbia. He talked about the great project of BOT: Build, own and then transfer back. This is a unique project. There has been no track history of this BOT, which is the jargon of build, own and transfer.
Let us assume that everything goes ahead and after 35 years it is transferred back to the government or the Canadian taxpayer who has helped foot the bill. Does the hon. parliamentary secretary not see the maintenance problems on a bridge over salt water?
A report this week said that there was an $18 million maintenance cost for the Lions Gate Bridge this year. He and I both know, having lived in British Columbia, that there is ongoing maintenance on bridges, especially over salt water. Is the Government of Canada going to get a 35-year old steel relic which the taxpayer paid for?
Regardless of all the interesting economic positives that he referred to on the island, how does the hon. parliamentary secretary rationalize what the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands said? She said that there was an environmental study commissioned in accordance with the Government of Canada's own laws.
There were hearings. However, as the parliamentary secretary must know, the summary and conclusions of the report mentioned by the hon. member for Saanich- Gulf Islands said that the admitted positives were outweighed by the negatives. The panel came out clearly and said not to proceed with the bridge.
It suggested more study of a tunnel or an improved ferry system so that the people of the island would still have their constitutional link.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for his question. I will try to cover all three points as quickly as possible.
I say the taxpayers will benefit because I sincerely believe they will. The ongoing costs of the ferry service are in the neighbourhood of $30 million or $32 million. If we are going to continue to provide the service the support of the federal government goes beyond the provision of the existing ferry link. There will be a time when new ferries must be built, and that is the responsibility of the federal government.
The subsidy is the long-term responsibility of the federal government, and it is calculated to be at $42 million a year. It is good for the taxpayer because the construction of the project will proceed on private enterprise funding. As the ferry service is removed the subsidy will be put into effect and will continue for 35 years.
That is the subsidy that the federal government would be responsible for anyway. We are providing the subsidy to fulfil the commitments we would have anyway. At the end of 35 years we would no longer have that commitment.
I say as a taxpayer of Canada, and as the member has pointed out as a taxpayer from the other part of the country, that is a good objective.
There are a number of differences from Lions Gate Bridge. If we had to go back to taking ferries across it would be untenable. A major difference in the design and structure is that the Lions Gate Bridge is steel. The bridge to Prince Edward Island is being designed to last
February 22, 1993

at least 100 years and is a concrete structure. It will not be subject to the same kind of weather.
The third question concerned the panel. The panel did recommend against proceeding, based on the assumption that there was a longer than two-day delay in the ice. However, it said its position would be different if it could be achieved within the two days and it made a number of recommendations. Since that time the government, the contractors, and the provinces have been proceeding following those recommendations to a letter.
No project has had more ongoing environmental reviews. There continue to be reviews and if it is not environmentally sound the project will not go ahead.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the parliamentary secretary how the government can proceed without doing an environmental assessment on this specific proposal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an ongoing assessment. It started with the generic but it is done on every stage this project has undergone.
The environmental considerations have been examined along with it and continue to be reviewed. As one of the commentators from the maritimes has put it, if we took all of the material that has been studied, printed, published, and written about the fixed link over time there would be enough material to put a solid link across the strait.
There has been and continues to be serious environmental assessment made at each stage of this project.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this very important debate today, particularly in view of the fact that I am from New Brunswick, which is one of the provinces that will be directly involved in the construction of this very important structure.
Much has been said about the economic and other benefits that will accrue to Prince Edward Island. Much should be said about them because not only will there be economic benefits to Prince Edward Island but there will be a significant spin-off effect to the entire province of New Brunswick, the entire Atlantic region, and to Canada as a whole, as was mentioned by the hon.
Government Orders
parliamentary secretary. I will attempt to deal with some of those matters.
I believe that the benefits are substantial and self-evident. However, we must look at the entire project on a much broader scale and come to terms with what it is going to mean to us as Canadians and to our reputation as a whole.
Canada has garnered an enviable reputation throughout the world for megaprojects on a grandiose scale. We only have to think of the SkyDome and the CN Tower in Toronto and now we will have this magnificent link between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
From India to China to the Philippines Canadians have been involved in major projects such as dams, power generation installations, roads, telecommunication networks and so on. As a result we as Canadians have garnered a super reputation throughout the world for our capacity to be able to deal with projects of this nature and to complete them successfully.
It has brought about a significant amount of self-respect and international respect for Canadians for our ability to tackle large and challenging projects. Make no mistake, this link is big by any world standards.
What we are talking about in the Northumberland Strait bridge will be the largest bridge that will have ever been built in North America.
Let us take a look at some of the pieces of equipment to demonstrate the magnitude of what we are speaking about. The crane that will be used to put the pieces of this project together will be 325 feet in height. It will be one of the largest cranes that will ever have been built in the world.
The bridge will require 200,000 tonnes of cement,
53,000	tonnes of reinforcing steel and 130,000 tonnes of asphalt. It will be built in 183 separate parts. When it is completed this structure will be 10 times as long as San Francisco's famous Golden Gate Bridge. The project will be watched, it will be studied and it will be envied by engineering firms and governments around the world.
The Strait Crossing Incorporated is a Canadian firm which has already earned an international reputation in the design of bridges and other such structures. As it is being undertaken by a firm of such international reputa-

Government Orders
tion this will only serve to strengthen Canada's reputation for engineering excellence.
I believe people will come from all over the world, just as they have for the other projects we have undertaken in this country. I have already mentioned the SkyDome and the CN Tower.
I believe that people will come from far and wide to see what it is that we are doing once again here in Canada, which has contributed so substantially to our reputation.
There is something about bridges that catches the public imagination. It is true that people rarely write songs or write poetically about sewers or pipelines but bridges are different. They do catch the imagination of people. It has happened in the past. They have caught the fancy of poets, writers and singers from time immemorial.
Perhaps that is because bridges speak to the human aspirations of each of us in reaching out for unattainable goals and objectives. They break down the barriers that separate us and bring people closer together. When this bridge is completed there is no question it will take its place as one of the greatest bridges in the entire world and that it will be one of the great engineering undertakings of the late 20th century.
There is no question that there are some lingering concerns on the part of some of the people of Prince Edward Island. It is perfectly understandable that some people are concerned about what sort of effect this project will have on their lives and on their culture. These are natural concerns but by no means unique.
As a case in point I mention the bridge that connects Oland Island in Sweden with the mainland. This bridge crosses the Baltic Sea. Some 25 years ago this same type of controversy occurred in that particular community in Sweden. That bridge was eventually built and is the largest bridge in Europe, although it will be less than half the size of the Northumberland Strait Crossing. Nonetheless, as with the P.E.I. crossing, that bridge was talked about and argued about for decades before construction actually took place. There was a lot of passionate dissension about the ramifications of the bridge from some quarters before construction began,
just as there has been in the case of the Northumberland Strait Crossing.
A Canadian government committee which studied the Oland bridge and a few other projects a few years ago found that it was virtually impossible to find anybody today on that island who is in disagreement with the fact that the project went ahead.
Any major commitment is to some extent a leap of faith. However this project has been carefully planned and carefully studied, and there has been a maximum of consultation with both the Government of Canada and the Government of Prince Edward Island. I know the Government of New Brunswick has also been consulted. Most important, there has been a maximum of consultation with the public involved. It is a sound and economically viable project. It is a sound and economically sensible project.
As I mentioned when I began my remarks, I look forward to the economic spin-offs for the province of Prince Edward Island and the adjacent province of New Brunswick. I ran through some of the figures about the amount of cement and steel and things of that nature which will be put into this bridge. I mentioned the size of the crane. In the short term, let alone the long term, this means jobs which are vitally important to all of our economies, particularly to Prince Edward Island at this crucial time and New Brunswick.
I can only say that besides the obvious advantages of having an important transportation link finally take place, which has been talked about for a good many years and which will take place after an extensive and exhaustive examination of the details of any problems that might occur, we have been assured that the concerns about the project can be put aside. I am happy to support this bill.
Although it is not a bill about whether we should go ahead with the construction of the link but rather a bill that will put in place the mechanics so that we can deal with the financing that will be required, I am delighted that this government has taken the initiative to ensure that this will become a reality.
I want to express appreciation on behalf of the people of New Brunswick, who will be extremely pleased when they have the opportunity to take part in the actual construction phase. I know that the people of Prince Edward Island will echo those words. It is a project of the
February 22, 1993

future and Canadians will benefit from it. It will happen in the very near future.

I listened with interest to the comments from my colleague, who is the chairman of the transport committee and a sailor of some note. I find it a bit disturbing that he is up in the House promoting a bridge that will replace a marine enterprise.
I want to raise with him the question of jobs. He will know that during the five-year construction phase of this bridge, should it come to be, roughly 1,000 jobs will be created. We heard the previous speaker talk about somewhere between 2,000 and 5,000 person-years of employment.
Can he explain why that is better than the 600 permanent maritime jobs that exist today for people on P.E.I. and in New Brunswick? Those jobs are going to be eliminated. Is he saying that it is more important to have
1,000	people working today for a short time than it is to have 600 people able to support their families not just for four years or five years but basically for a lifetime?
That is really the trade-off between these two. Is he saying that he supports the elimination of these 600 maritime jobs just so 1,000 construction workers can be employed for a little while?

Mr. Speaker, the workers at Marine Atlantic will know, not only because of my fondness for maritime traditions and the sea but also because of the excellent service they and Marine Atlantic have given the residents of Prince Edward Island and the travelling public over the years, of the efforts that I have exerted on their behalf to ensure the continuity of those jobs.
I believe with substantial confidence that Marine Atlantic will work to ensure that a significant number of the 600 jobs the hon. member is referring to-although I am not certain that figure is not a little on the high side-will be assimilated into other phases and areas of the work place, either with Marine Atlantic or in the operation of the bridge after it is completed.
We are looking at the passing of an era. There is no question about that. What we are replacing it with is an opportunity for additional industry and additional infrastructure, whether it be in tourism or related areas either
Government Orders
in Prince Edward Island or in New Brunswick. There will be the creation of an infrastructure to support the bridge. It is possible that an entirely new community may be developed just somewhat north of Cape Tormentine, which will also provide opportunities for additional jobs.
In the final analysis, if one did a model of the economic scale we would come to the conclusion that not only will the majority of the workers who the hon. member has expressed a concern for-and I know that concern to be genuine having served with him on the transport committee and know that he is very dedicated to the community that he represents-will not only be assimilated into new and exciting jobs and possibilities but that many more hundreds of jobs will become evident as we proceed with the project and the project becomes a reality.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to ask a question. I appreciate the hon. member's prowess on the high seas. I also know that he is a very real fiscal Conservative who really does not like to sugar-coat the public with a lot of false numbers when it comes to taxes and costs of projects.
I admit full well all the glowing things he said about the magnitude of the project, no one is denying that. Obviously many people on the island believe it is going to be an asset in terms of construction. Obviously it is going to provide jobs. Does he not think in this time of fiscal restraint, when the government is saying it does not have money for so many things that are laudable, that there is a little hocus-pocus going on here when there is almost a $220 million difference between the subsidy that is going to this private enterprise and the cost to the ferries?
He is the chairman of the transport committee. I have certainly had experience on that committee. The average is anywhere from $21 million to $29 million and it has been going down. The average now is $29 million and yet the subsidy is going to be $42 million for 35 years. Without getting into the subsidy, I would like him to state what it means in terms of his taxpayers and to come clean on this thing. Part of my problem with this project is the sugar-coating of the real costs and the fact that the public taxpayer is going to be involved, not only in the construction but in a continuing way.

The minister who introduced the bill said that it was an $800 million project. The parliamentary secretary said today that it was an $850 million project. I would like to remind the hon. member, since I imagine he is aware of the study of 1987, that Woods Gordon said that the project was going to cost $1.3 billion. Does the member honestly think that the costs of a project from six years ago are going to go down? Why are we concentrating on $800 million to $850 million for the project? The main study that justified this approach in 1987 from Woods Gordon, and I can give the quote which I hope to do when I make my speech, estimated that it was going to $1,311 million.
If we are going to face facts and be realistic with Canadians, let us not tell them that it is not going to cost any money. How can you say it is not going to cost any money when you do not agree that there is such an error in the estimate of the cost of the project?

Mr. Speaker, there was a lot of substance in what the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants asked. Since I can no longer see a clock opposite me, I am not certain I have time to answer everything that was asked. I will seek your guidance as to just how much time I have to deal with it.
To begin with, I have no reason to doubt that the figures that have been projected as the final costs by the firm that has put together the bid on this project will indeed be the final costs.
I have already expressed to the House how pleased I am that this engineering firm of international stature was the consortium that was successful in having its bid to construct this megaproject accepted by the federal government. This did not come about overnight nor did it come without a substantial amount of study and investigation on the part of the people responsible for the fiscal purse.
I think we have to hearken back to the comments that were made by the parliamentary secretary when he reminded the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants that not only must we take into account the annual subsidies that are paid for the ferry crossing, but we must take into account the capitalization of those particular pieces of infrastructure that are in place, including the docking facilities, wharfage, the vessels and any other infrastructure that is currently required such as the toll
booths and the parking areas, all of which require not only maintenance but replacement sooner rather than later. We are not talking about penny-ante stuff here. We are talking about replacement of a vessel which is going to cost tens of millions of dollars. Over a period of 35 years, forgetting about the built-in guarantees that are not only held in performance bonds that are required by the contractor but actual cash that is in the kitty, this particular infrastructure not only will be maintained and operated for the amount of dollars that they suggest they are going to be, but at the end of the 35 year period will be passed over to the taxpayers of this country with a guarantee that the condition will be substantial enough to carry it through to the 100-year peak.
The hon. member is absolutely correct. I am concerned. I am a fiscal Conservative. I feel that in the total picture of things this is going to be a boon for the taxpayers rather than a burden.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having the opportunity to speak at second reading of this bill today. I do so because of a strong belief that what this government is doing is wrong. That is a belief that is based not just on my assessment as a transport critic for my caucus, but is based on discussions I have had with people in P.E.I., the New Democratic Party on the island, friends of the island, labour leaders and others who are really concerned about a number of elements of this proposal.
Let me put this into a very personal context. A moment ago I raised with the chairman of the transport committee the question of jobs. When we talk about jobs, it seems like it is sort of a broad label. We do not talk about Joe Smith or Mary Smith by name. Let me bring it down to a local level.
In terms of the marine Atlantic employment on P.E.I., here are the communities and here is the payroll. It is the impact on these communities, not just at the funnel where the bridge will go but throughout the community.
Wilmot has 14 workers with a payroll of $436,000. Wellington has 11 workers with a payroll of $432,000. Summerside has 89 workers with a payroll of $2.6 million. St. Eleanors has 30 workers with a payroll of $895,000. Miscouche has 13 workers with a payroll of $513,000. Kin kora has 26 workers with a payroll of
February 22, 1993

$750,000. Kensington has 19 workers with a payroll of $646,000. Crapaud has 14 workers with a payroll of $513,000. Cornwall has 29 workers with a payroll of $1,037,000. Charlottetown has 42 workers with a payroll of $1.4 million and Borden has 115 workers and their families with a payroll of $3 million.
That puts it into context. These are real people and real communities. They are going to lose their jobs because they are not construction workers. While some may currently be employed in the collection of cash and the selling of tickets and may logically move into employment with the bridge operator, I know of nothing that is written in ink and signed by lawyers and verified, no legal proof that guarantees any of these jobs for the current workers.
Certainly on the fishery side, even though there is talk about some kind of fund-a figure of $10 million has been used-there is no guarantee that will work or that there will be anything for them to do if the fishery is destroyed.
Let us take a look at the numbers. I want to run through them again. The estimates we have heard in this House and elsewhere suggest that on the construction side we have a five year period when the work will proceed, anywhere from 2,000, 3,000 to 5,000 person-years of employment, or roughly working out to 1,000 construction jobs. Clearly there are spin-off jobs as well because the suppliers of steel, gravel and concrete all have part of that. Quite frankly I am not sure if that is included in the 1,000 or if it is over and above the 1,000.
Compare that to what exists today: somewhere in the range of between 500 and 600 ferry workers, good paying jobs, union jobs primarily but also some non-union jobs, jobs that have kept those people and their families alive, jobs that they were thinking about retiring from, whether it is in 5 years, 10 years or 20 years, depending on where you are on the seniority list. If this project goes through, they are gone. We know that the unemployment rate on P.E.I. is one of the higher ones in our provinces, so on one hand we can understand why government, whether it is the federal government or the provincial government of P.E.I., is looking for employment opportunities. That is what we are here for, to try and assist in the
Government Orders
development of greater opportunities for people to work.
What we are seeing with this project is that those permanent jobs are going. They are out the door. They are over the side. There will be some temporary replacements over five years for the construction. I do not know what the numbers are for the operating side, but I would suspect it is not 600.1 would suspect it is not 500, not 400. Perhaps in committee that is one of the things we can get answered so that we can have everything on the table and know what we are dealing with.
P.E.I. itself is not going to be the great beneficiary of those construction jobs. The estimates I have seen show a range of 9 per cent to 35 per cent of those construction jobs going to residents of P.E.I. The rest one would assume would start in New Brunswick, but also elsewhere in Atlantic Canada, and who knows where else in Canada those jobs will go. Quite frankly, there will be people who want those jobs because people are hurting out there.
P.E.I. is not going to be the beneficiary to the same degree as other parts of the country. That is the job side. I have not even touched the fisheries workers and the impact on them and the numbers and the families. Nor have I touched on the environment. My colleagues who have spoken before me have dealt with those issues, so I am going to deal with other aspects of the process.
Let us take a look at the dollars and cents. We have had some questions and answers about that already, but let me put it in the context of what they are paying now and what we are going to be paid if this project goes forward.
Currently the cost of operating the ferries is around $41 million. About $17 million of that comes from fares. That is what the people who use the ferries pay to transport themselves and their vehicle across the strait.
The taxpayers' subsidy is roughly $24 million. Quite frankly, Marine Atlantic has done very well in terms of reducing the level of subsidy. In 1988, for example, it was $24.4 million. In 1989 it was down to $22.6 million. In 1990 it was back up slightly, to $23.8 million.

Government Orders
Revenues are moving up very well. In 1988 total fare revenues for both services were $13.9 million. They moved up to $15.1 million in 1989, and by 1990 they were at $17.1 million for a total cost of $40.9 million. Marine Atlantic was doing very well in raising their revenues.
We have $24 million from the federal government and $17 million from the passengers, for a total of $41 million. This proposal for the fixed link for the bridge will require, we are told, in addition to the private capital an ongoing operating subsidy from the federal government of $42 million a year for the next 35 years.
The parliamentary secretary talked about how in the long term that was going to save money. Even though we are going to be paying out more, in fact we are going to be paying out the equivalent of the amount that the users of the ferry are paying now, an additional $17 million a year, at the end of the 35 years that subsidy will stop. I assume that is when the bridge will become ours, that is the taxpayers of Canada, as part of the BOT that my friend from Annapolis Valley-Hants was talking about. That is one way to look at it.
Currently for those 35 years we are going to be paying out an extra $600 million. We are going to save money by spending $600 million more. That is an interesting perspective. If we were to keep the ferries in operation, that $600 million would provide another 17 years of subsidy, assuming the same level, on top of 35 years.
I do not expect to be here in another 50-odd years but that money would provide ferry services to Prince Edward Island beyond my lifetime.
The other aspect of this financing, and it was mentioned again in some of the government's speeches, is that you have to re-equip. It is an aging fleet and at some point we have to replace those ferries. Friends of the Island would argue we should be adding to the fleet right now to improve service, eliminate line-ups and delays. Those are some of the economic negatives of the current system.
It has been calculated that if we replace the equipment now because of the 35-year life span, the subsidy would only go up to $25 million a year assuming we bought offshore from Korea, Brazil or Japan. Unfortunately
there are not many places left in Canada where we build ships and certainly the vast majority of the ships we build are government sponsored ships. It would be $1.2 million extra because it would be amortized over the 35-year pay-back period. If we were able to produce the ship in Canada the subsidy required would be $28.5 million.
It would cost more, but a $28.5 million subsidy is still a lot less than a $42 million subsidy which this government is prepared to pay for the next 35 years to provide a fixed link to Prince Edward Island. That does not include what it is going to cost us when we accept responsibility for the bridge.
There was some dialogue back and forth that this is a concrete, not steel bridge and therefore one cannot compare it to others. In one of my previous occupations I was a construction inspector for the Ontario Department of Highways. I supervised the construction of bridges. I did the concrete. I did the steel.
I was involved in supervising the building of a bridge in Thunder Bay which was completed around 1968-69, roughly 22 years ago. For the last two years they have been pulling off the old concrete. They have been replacing the walls along the side and have redone the deck. Do you know why, Mr. Speaker? The road salt in Thunder Bay ate away at the concrete and reinforcing steel. That is after 21 or 22 years over fresh water.
What is the cost going to be to the taxpayer 35 years from now for a bridge that has been operated by those in the private sector? They will minimize as much as possible the maintenance they do, particularly the structural maintenance, because they know in another 5 or 10 years it will not be their problem any more. They are going to give short shrift to any replacement of the abutment walls, guardrails or driving surface and the taxpayers will be stuck with the tab.
We cannot just look at the dollars and cents today. It is our job to anticipate the future costs to the taxpayers. That is what we are elected to do. If we do not look at that, or if we turn a blind eye to it and say: "let us go for it, we need a quick fix, we need a quick pre-election hit in terms of jobs in P.E.I., New Brunswick and elsewhere", then we are selling the taxpayers short.
February 22, 1993

At the same time and perhaps it is not so much for me to say as someone who comes from P.E.I., but I think a fixed link to Prince Edward Island will change that island.
There are the psychological and sociological implications; the raison d'etre of P.E.I. and the lifestyle. There is a transition and whether one flies in or goes by ferry, there is not the rushing in there on four wheels with the intensity we find elsewhere in Canada.
I have been to P.E.I. a number times. It is quite a remarkable part of this country. I think a fixed link will destroy that. Only time will tell what P.E.I. will become, but it will never be the same. We have to recognize that too. As one letter to the editor suggested: "Do not forget, there is a reason why it is called Prince Edward Island". We have to be cognizant of that.
The plebiscite was held and slightly more than 50 per cent voted in favour of a fixed link. They did not vote in favour of a bridge. They did not vote in favour of a tunnel. They voted in favour of some kind of fixed link.
My community had a similar experience in terms of how plebiscites can be used for the purposes for which they are designed and that is to get your own way. Back in 1969 the province of Ontario forced the amalgamation of the former cities of Port Arthur, Fort William, Neebing and McIntyre. We had a plebiscite to change the name. That is much different and much less important than whether or not there is a bridge between P.E.I. and New Brunswick but I think the example stands.
We had a choice between Lakehead, The Lakehead and Thunder Bay. As this House knows, if there are three elements in an election the result is a split vote. More people voted for a combination of Lakehead and The Lakehead than Thunder Bay, but Thunder Bay was the top of the list and that is our name.
In the same way, the plebiscite that was put out was ambiguous. It did not say: "Are you in favour of a bridge? Are you in favour of a tunnel? Are you against any form of fixed link?" That would have been the fair way.
Government Orders
Prince Edward Island New Democrats have continued to call for a second plebiscite to see whether or not there is support for the bridge type of a fixed link. I suspect the vast majority in that province would say no to it.
It is extremely important that the committee hear witnesses. It is unusual for a legislative committee, but we have a moral responsibility to the people of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick to have committee meetings in those provinces. It is their way of life. Regardless of what I may think or of what I may feel it is going to affect them. It is not going to affect me in Thunder Bay. The committee has a responsibility to hold public hearings on the island and in New Brunswick so we can hear both sides of the question. Then we can come back to Ottawa and deal with the question of the legislation itself and any amendments required that affect whether or not it is passed through this House.
It is an important issue. I believe this House has a responsibility to follow through in that way. I also believe this House has a responsibility to say no to this bill, vote it down when it comes up for a vote tonight and make sure we put an end to this idea once and for all.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a pleasure for me to take part in this debate. I have been waiting for this debate for many years.
Bill C-110 provides the authority to enter into agreements and provides financing agreements to allow the fixed link to go ahead between the province of New Brunswick and the province of Prince Edward Island.
I have an unique perspective on this because I live exactly at the intersection between the province of Prince Edward Island, the province of Nova Scotia and the province of New Brunswick. I have relatives, friends and business acquaintances in each province and I often deal back and forth. I am very much affected by interprovincial trade barriers.
The Northumberland Strait is probably the biggest interprovincial trade barrier we have in the maritime provinces.
Many people consider this fixed link as a stand alone project. In my view as an Atlantic Canadian member of Parliament who is very much committed to Atlantic Canada and believes in it, we cannot compete. We can never pull ourselves up to take part in the strength of the

Government Orders
Canadian economy without a proper transportation system. The proper transportation system must include a fixed link between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
I would like to ask members to think about something. On one side of the Northumberland Strait is Prince Edward Island and on the other side is New Brunswick. They both share the same work ethic. They both have the same resources available and the same opportunities.
On one side of that body of water in Prince Edward Island, the unemployment rate is 16.2 per cent. On the New Brunswick side of that body of water it is 12.1 per cent. The only difference is a transportation handicap for P.E.I.
I hear some members talking about jobs lost on the ferries and competing with jobs during construction. To me that is just the tip of the iceberg. The jobs lost because P.E.I. is not competitive are in the thousands, not in the hundreds.
We talk about hundreds of ferry workers and hundreds of fixed link workers but the fact is that with an unemployment rate of 16.2 per cent P.E.I. has thousands of unemployed it would not have if its people had the same opportunities as those of New Brunswick. As an over-all concept and project for Atlantic Canada it is an integral part of our transportation system.
I compared the unemployment rate in P.E.I. with the unemployment rate in New Brunswick and it is just going to get worse. Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have identified transportation, and specifically highway construction as the most important economic development tool we have.
Put aside all economic development incentives, regional development programs and everything else. If we in Atlantic Canada do not have a viable transportation system we will not achieve our goals no matter how much money is put into our area. Without transportation we cannot compete.
Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have acknowledged that. They have made every effort and are going to spend hundreds of millions of dollars on our TransCanada highway. If P.E.I. is left isolated without the fixed link, it will just slip further behind. Instead of having an unemployment rate difference between 16.1 per cent and 12.1 per cent, it will get even worse as the economies of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick improve.
Of all the three maritime provinces, P.E.I. has the lowest average income. The only province with a higher unemployment rate and lower average income has longer ferries, and that is Newfoundland. Perhaps there is some connection between the length of ferries, unemployment rates and average income.
For P.E.I. to become part of our economy and take its appropriate place we must have a fixed link. The fixed link is just a part of our total approach to transportation. We spend a lot of time here asking the federal government to help finance highways in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick because we know that is where our future is.
Without the fixed link as an integral part of our area we will not have the transportation system we need to go into the coming decades with global competition the way it is.
As a business person in Atlantic Canada living right at the intersection of the three provinces, I can attest to the handicap because of the ferry system. Maybe the ferry system is the best in the world but it still means hours and hours of delay if one is shipping a product or on a service call. It means inconsistency mostly.
Many people say it takes an hour to catch a ferry but that is not the case. Often people will wait three or four hours. If someone is trying to compete by shipping products or providing a service there is inconsistency and potential delays.
I talked to a major manufacturer's representative from central Canada this summer. He had approached me about a project in regional development and was visiting all three maritime provinces. He had just come from Prince Edward Island and had been caught in one of those line-ups at the ferries.
Without assessing it or talking to the provincial authorities or anyone, he knew he could not compete if he had to face that transportation handicap. He left the island without even a consultation and visited New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. I predict that he will set up a manufacturing facility in one of those areas. It was the transportation link handicap between New Brunswick and P.E.I. that drove him away.
February 22, 1993

In summary, certainly for the economy of Atlantic Canada we must have an up-to-date, modern transportation system throughout the whole region, and that includes a fixed link as an integral part.

If I am not mistaken, there have been seven environmental studies performed on this project. The major environmental study-

Mr. Speaker, early this month I was advised in writing by the House of Commons that my main budget for 1993-94 would be increased by 3.16 per cent, pursuant to the economic and fiscal statement made on December 2, 1992 by the Minister of Finance. This represents an increase of $5,290 which I refuse to accept, speaking on behalf of Canadian taxpayers.
According to the notes on Bill C-113 provided by the Department of Employment and Immigration the purpose of these amendments is to limit unemployment insurance spending to an amount equal to 57 per cent of weekly earnings, in other words, a cut of 3 per cent for Canadian workers.
The purpose of my decision today is to limit my spending for the sake of Canadian taxpayers.

Mr. Speaker, a report by Le Journal de Montreal today projects a loss of $490 million for the Montreal area economy alone between 1990 and 1994 from this government's legislative changes to unemployment insurance. This loss of purchasing power is devastating to small business, creating a spin-off of job losses that will be most severe for women and young people.
The minister suggests that cutting UI benefits from 60 per cent to 57 per cent and depriving anyone who has quit or been fired from receiving benefits will save the taxpayer money.
The government had better wake up to the fact that the taxpayer will actually pay more if these ill-conceived cuts to UI are not withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, in 1987 the House debated a motion that would have allowed the state to use capital punishment. I voted in favour of the motion because I believed that the state should have the option to execute anyone convicted of first degree murder. Today my position remains the same.
The present law provides that anyone convicted of first degree murder will be sentenced to life imprisonment without parole for 25 years. However, it is troubling that a person convicted of several first degree murders is also eligible for parole after only 25 years.
Therefore I call upon the government to bring forward amendments to the Criminal Code that will ensure anyone found guilty of more than one first degree murder charge will serve a minimum of 25 years for each conviction and that all first degree murder sentences will be ineligible for judicial review.

Mr. Speaker, Canada Post seems to have lost its sense of why it exists. Service to Canadians has always been and should continue to be the primary function of this Crown corporation.

February 22, 1993
However, the latest misguided practice announced by Canada Post leads Canadians to believe that corporation's drive for profits has pushed aside common sense. If a letter is mailed to the wrong address Canada Post will not permit Canadians to simply alter the address and send it along. Instead, we are to pay for a new envelope and a 43-cent stamp to redirect the letter or the letter could be returned to the sender.
If Canada Post showed common sense it would permit delivery to the correct address rather than going back to the sender. There would be no difference in the cost regardless of the letter's destination. Current policies are being designed to fleece Canadians, not to serve them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, February is heart month. Three million Canadians suffer from cardiovascular disease. Every year, about 75,000 Canadians die as a result of heart disease or a stroke.
This government is proud of the fact that Canadian scientists have led the way in the progress that has been achieved in the treatment of cardiovascular disease. Thanks to their discoveries and improvements in preventive care, the percentage of deaths due to heart disease and strokes among Canadians under 65 has dropped by 36 per cent since 1955.
Under its national health research and development Program, the Department of National Health and Welfare funds the heart health initiative launched with provincial governments and other partners, including the Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada and volunteer and professional organizations in the health sector. The federal government will spend nearly $13 million on this initiative over five years.
Furthermore, during the past five years the Medical Research Council has awarded about $79 million for cardiovascular research.
There are still major challenges to be met, since this type of disease is the main cause of death in Canada. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you will join me in wishing them good luck during heart month.

Mr. Speaker, it has been brought to my attention by one of my constituents that the Government of Sweden is now developing new regulations for radiation exposure which are expected to be between two and ten milligauss. This came about as a result of studies which found that children exposed to a field of two milligauss from power lines have a threefold increase in their cancer risk, while children exposed to three milligauss have a fourfold increase in their risk of cancer.
In another study carried out in Denmark it was found that people exposed to three milligauss are 64 per cent more likely to develop leukaemia.
In summary, the evidence revealed that chronic exposure to weak electromagnetic fields of two to three milligauss may cause fatal sickness.
At present the Government of Canada uses a set of guidelines developed by the International Radiation Protection Association of 1,000 milligauss for public exposure and 5,000 milligauss for occupational exposure.
Without commenting on the merit of the European studies, I am calling on the government to examine these findings and, if needed, to develop new radiation standards to ensure the protection of our citizens.

Mr. Speaker, jobs, jobs, jobs. Over 550 new jobs have been created since 1990 at Goodyear in Napanee. These are high-tech, well-paid jobs, created to supply state of the art automotive tires to North American and European markets.
Goodyear would like to expand its facility creating up to another 450 jobs. This new expansion is being threatened due to the high cost of electricity which has increased over 40 per cent in the past four years. This increase in electrical rates not only affects our competi-
February 22, 1993

tive position to export but also threatens all small businesses and places serious burdens on home owners.
I urge the Government of Ontario and its Crown corporation, Ontario Hydro, to honour the verbal agreement and forecasts made to Goodyear that rates would not increase past the rate of inflation.

Mr. Speaker, as the implementation of the North American free trade agreement grows nearer this government's blarney blossoms like a wild flower. In fact if the collective noses of the Tory cabinet were to grow like Pinocchio's there would be no need for the fixed link to P.E.I.
A cursory cosy review done by internal federal bureaucrats is now hailed as a full environmental assessment. Wrong. The language of the NAFTA is now claiming to guarantee that countries will not lower environmental standards to attract investment. Wrong. In the latest twist, environmental regulations are being reviewed to ensure that they will not hinder trade or do not exceed those of our other trading partners. In short, get out of the way we are levelling the playing field.
Incredibly the regulations under review cover such sensitive areas as ozone depleting substances, transportation and storage of hazardous chemicals, pulp mill effluent and ocean dumping.
This government has fundamentally failed to understand the concerns of average Canadians, people who are looking for increased safety and health regulations, not the abandonment of our air, land and water to a dangerous chemical cocktail.

Mr. Speaker, because of a presentation in my riding I missed the debate on Bill S-8.1 would like to put some concerns on record about it.
Bill S-8 does not address the double standard applied to motor vehicles in Canada, depending on whether the car came through the American system or the Canadian
system. Essentially a Canadian car meets the Canadian standard and U.S. cars must meet the American standard with some upgrades, but they are not the same.
In principle I do not think Americans should be allowed to sell products in Canada that Canadians are restricted from selling by law. From a consumer's standpoint the result will be a diluted and inconsistent safety recall notice procedure. From a competitiveness point of view the Canadian car industry is required to meet more expensive standards than its competition from the U.S. I will be working to establish one safety standard for vehicles in Canada, no matter where they came from, through contacts in the Department of Transport.

Mr. Speaker, Don Lander, president of Canada Post Corporation at a salary of almost $300,000 a year, has found yet another new way to infuriate Canadians when it comes to the delivery of mail.
Canada Post says that if a letter is delivered to you in error it is now your responsibility to place it in a new envelope, re-address it, pay for the stamp, and put it back in the mail.
The hon. member for South Shore makes the following statement:
It is nonsense. It is an outrage with which Canadians will simply
not put up, nor should they. This measure will not result in Canada
Post getting its revenues in order. It will simply result in a lot of mail
being thrown out that should be delivered.
I agree with my colleague opposite. This proposal should now be redirected to the garbage bin or, to quote a minister's look-alike, returned to sender.

Mr. Speaker, my constituents are concerned about the safety of their communities. Like many Canadians they have lost faith in the criminal justice system. They believe that it places the rights of offenders above the protection of society.

February 22, 1993
The Minister of Justice and the Solicitor General are to be commended for the parole reforms which they have initiated. Praise for these reforms comes from many sources including my constituents.
Most first-time non-violent offenders respond well to rehabilitation and reintegrate fully into society. My constituents' concern however is about the violent, repeat and sexual offenders. Occasionally an offender is released from prison even though corrections officials know the offender is still dangerous to society.
I urge the Solicitor General to pursue actively the option of keeping designated dangerous offenders in prison beyond the end of their sentences and expanding the definition and use of serious harm provisions.
This solution would protect the public from those very few truly dangerous individuals who simply cannot be rehabilitated.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the city of Sudbury has passed a resolution requesting that the federal government reverse its decision to freeze grants in lieu of taxes to municipalities.
Canadian municipalities are crying foul over this government's back door approach to passing on debt time and time again.
The federal government has arbitrarily and without consultation decided to freeze these grants at 1992 levels and has proposed to amend the formula for calculating these grants.
As a result the city of Sudbury along with all other Canadian municipalities is faced with a combined loss of $80 million in the next two years, which will show up as a savings on the federal books.
One level of government cannot pride itself on tackling the debt by passing it on to another level whenever it suits it. Canadian debt is owed by all Canadians no matter at what level. It is time this government took responsibility for its share of the debt and co-operated with all other levels of government to deal with the serious problem of the total level of debt we face as Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my constituents from Cariboo-Chilcotin I want to pay tribute to a truly great Canadian.
I recall the first time I met Joe Clark back in the early 1970s on one of his several visits to the Cariboo. We stood together leaning over the snake fence that surrounded the stampede grounds. That conversation was the first of many, and the more I got to know my colleague the more I came to respect him.
Joe Clark is a man whose love of his country has earned him respect from coast to coast, but it goes beyond his love of country. In an era where nearly all politicians are held in low esteem Joe Clark has been one politician who is seen by the people of Canada as having retained his honesty and integrity.
Joe Clark will be missed by his colleagues on the Hill and he will be equally missed by the many Canadians whose lives he has touched. The people of Cariboo- Chilcotin wish him well.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to challenge the government's phantom increase in merchandise exports to the United States.
The government claims that our merchandise exports to the United States have risen 11 per cent and this is the greatest surge in exports since 1984.
I cannot help but notice that the Canadian dollar dropped in value relative to the U.S. currency by 10 per cent, more than any single year since the 1970s.
This of course means that a Canadian product sold in American markets and in U.S. dollars brought 10 per cent more in Canadian in December 1992 than it did in December 1991. A Canadian exporter can realize a 10 per cent increase in sales value without any increase in sales volume.
This kind of export increase means no increase in jobs or standard of living for Canadians. While these export increases are phantoms the job losses, the business closures and the capital flight have been all too real for millions of Canadians. While we cannot blame all of

February 22, 1993

Oral Questions
Canada's woes on free trade, we can observe that while Canada is not working neither is free trade, nor are the Tory and Liberal parties that embrace it.

Mr. Speaker, many of my constituents have written to me concerning the sales of so-called serial killer cards. These cards are allowed into Canada. They object strongly to the distribution of them.
Card collecting has been a pastime for young people for decades, but killer cards salute and extol those who inflict pain and death. Many Canadians consider these cards to be potentially harmful to the development of their children.
I wrote to the Minister of National Revenue on this issue and was greatly disappointed today to receive a letter in which he says that only one of three series of killer cards examined by his department meet the provisions of the Criminal Code of Canada in terms of obscenity and will be banned.
I urge the government to review the legislation which is obviously out of date so that it will reflect the majority view that these killer cards are obscene and should be banned from importation into Canada.

Mr. Speaker, our trade figures for 1992 are out and they look pretty good. In fact, they are so good they should be placed on the record.
As reported in Friday's front page article in The Financial Post, exports reached an all-time high in 1992, $157 billion, an increase of 11 per cent over 1991.
As well, our exports to the United States are up, as is our trade surplus with the United States. In fact, our over-all trade surplus increased by $1.8 billion over 1991 and the numbers are looking even better for this year.
I think our policies are working.

eliminate violence in our society and thus protect our children and give all citizens a better quality of life.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition to present today that has been certified as to form and content.
The petitioners state that on November 24, 1989 the House of Commons unanimously passed a motion stating:
That this House express its concern for the more than one million
Canadian children currently living in poverty and seek to achieve the
goal of eliminating poverty among Canadian children by the year
2000.
Poverty among children inhibits learning and preparation for employment, constituting a cost to future national productivity. Sound national financial management demands the prevention of poverty. Child poverty is a fundamental reality of family poverty. Canada has ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child and has a moral obligation to seek the elimination of child poverty in Canada. A political commitment to eliminate child poverty in Canada requires public commitment and initiative among broad sectors of the Canadian population at local and national levels.
Therefore the undersigned humbly pray and call upon Parliament to take the actions necessary to reaffirm its commitment to seek the elimination of poverty among children in Canada by the year 2000 and to develop a plan for the implementation of this commitment.

Mr. Speaker, I have three sets of petitions to present today.
The first one calls upon Parliament to understand that many studies have shown a link between violence and entertainment and desensitization to violence in our society; that hundreds of women, men and children, including seniors and the disabled, are killed every year by an increasing number of people who state that they got the idea from something they saw or who did not grasp and respect the humanity of their victims; that we are increasingly becoming a culture of violence and violence has become an ordinary part of our children's lives; that part of this culture is a game called the serial killer board game; and that the laws of Canada do not

February 22, 1993

deal with this material portraying torture, rape and murder as fun.

This petition is signed by almost 500 people in my community of New Westminster-Burnaby.

The
second petition, Mr. Speaker, is signed by people from right across Canada. It has almost 1,200 signatures.
It calls upon the government to continue the six-month interest-free period for repayment of Canada student loans following graduation. It also calls upon Parliament to reverse the decision regarding the requirements for full-time student status and to define a full-time student as one who carries a 60 per cent course load.
As well it calls upon Parliament not to remove the six-month interest-free period on student loans and to withdraw the legislation, reverting to the principles of the Family Allowance Act, and not discriminate against those parents who are students and also use the Canada Student Loans Program.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition from my constituents asking Parliament to amend the Divorce Act so that a mother or father, unless there is serious cause, could be prevented from placing obstacles in the relationship between a child and the child's grandparents. In other words, they ask that
the act be amended so that it would be illegal for a parent to obstruct the relationship between a child and the child's grandparents.
They petition for further amendments to the act that would give a grandparent who is granted access to a child the right to make inquiries and be given information as to the health, education and welfare of the grandchild.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to present a petition today pursuant to Standing Order 36. This petition is regarding the CBC.
The petitioners ask that Parliament recognize the tools for building a better Canada have been abandoned by this Parliament; that important national institutions have been underfunded and then privatized; and that the government has cut CBC funding by $140 million over the next four years, resulting in 1,200 job losses and the closing of 10 regional stations in Calgary, Comer Brook, Goose Bay, Sydney, Sept lies, Toronto, Saskatoon and Windsor, as well as other areas.
I am particularly interested in this matter because Victoria, a city that is close to me, is the only capital city in Canada that is not provided with CBC radio service. I agree with the petition.
The petitioners urge the government to consider restoring proper funding to the CBC so that it can fulfil its mandate and its role as the heartbeat of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have an extensive petition that I would like to summarize.
These petitioners point out that a great number of Canadian youths who belong to middle and lower-income families are drawn out of schools at an early age due to the present financial difficulty.
They urge the government to invest in Canada's future by promoting a better educational program for students and to prepare them for global competitiveness.
The petitioners make a number of recommendations and I will summarize them very briefly. They want the reformation of the income tax law to allow middle and

lower-income parents to claim their children as dependants under certain circumstances.
They want the elimination of the goods and services tax on students' books and school supplies. They want the promotion of subsidies at the post-secondary level. They want the promotion of price control on text books and vital school supplies. They want the promotion of job training opportunities and programs for future graduates.
They want the promotion of job creation and implementation of assistance programs. They want provisions of incentives for youths to improve themselves through better education and training. They want leniency by the Secretary of State toward students whose student loans are due and who cannot afford to repay them because they have no job.
Finally, they urge the Secretary of State to involve students in all policies that affect them and Canada.
