Mr. Speaker, at the conclusion of my remarks before Question Period I was addressing the economics of the fixed link.
February 22, 1993

I just wanted to summarize my earlier remarks. The fixed link will eliminate an impediment to trade among the three provinces of P.E.I., Nova Scotia and New Brunswick when it is completed. There certainly is now an impediment to transportation and economic development.
The Northumberland Strait is a body of water between P.E.I. and New Brunswick. On one side of that body of water the unemployment rate is 16.2 per cent and on the other side it is 12.1 per cent. The only difference is that P.E.I. has the disadvantage of the poor transportation system between the two.
I started to address some of the environmental concerns that have been brought up over the years. I had mentioned that it had gone through seven environmental studies, the most complete of which addressed the ice-out situation. It recommended that, based on an estimate of a seven-day delay due to ice-outs, the project not go ahead.
A more specific study was done on that problem which addressed it based on a generic type of fixed link that is being proposed now. It arrived at the conclusion that that type of bridge would well meet the criteria of a two-day delay ice-out period. In fact, the period under the present plan is considered to be substantially less than the two days required by the environmental process.
The way they plan to build the bridge is interesting. They plan to build as much of it on land as possible and then take the assemblies out and place them in the water. There will be some dredging taking place during construction but there will be little. There will be less than there is now in the Northumberland Strait over a two-year period, and the bridge will be constructed over five years. Therefore, in terms of upsetting the fishery or the environment, there will be far less dredging than is being done now.
Again the design is veiy unique. It is very interesting that they have decided to build almost all of it on Prince Edward Island.
The impact on fishing will be addressed. During construction there will be a small impact on the fishery. There have been offsets put in place for the fishermen. A subject that nobody talks about is the advantage to the fishery when it is completed. There is a good chance the
Government Orders
fishery will be enhanced. Anywhere there has been a man-made structure like the fixed link with a large amount of construction being done under water as in Canso or Bar Harbour, Maine the fishery ends up being concentrated on these structures. It creates a natural habitat for lobsters and other fish after completion of the project, which runs contrary to the argument that it may upset the fishery.
Another point that is not understood is that the ferries that go between New Brunswick and P.E.I. are allotted a wide swath from P.E.I. to New Brunswick in which there is no fishing allowed at present. It is a large area and it will be eliminated. When the bridge is completed that area will be given back to the fishery again.
There probably will be a small negative impact on the fishery during construction. However a lot of people, including myself, think there will be a much larger positive impact after the project is completed. Some people suggest there will be a battle among the fishermen over the 44 abutments of the bridge. They will each want to have one or two. I expect that will be an interesting procedure.
I have attended many presentations by the president of Strait Crossing Incorporated. Mr. Giannelia has gone out of his way time and time again to meet with people in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and P.E.I. He will meet with anyone, he will answer any questions or concerns and he accepts advice and direction at all of his meetings. I am impressed by the way he handles questions. There is no time limit. He will take as much time as is required and is not afraid to touch any subject. He has thought this out, is very determined to go ahead with it and is determined to meet the time guidelines as outlined. Every aspect of the project has been addressed from an environmental perspective and every part has had its environmental impact addressed. It will be considered at the time of construction.
I live in one of the communities that is closest to it on the mainland side, Amherst, Nova Scotia. It is a very big and important project for us. Many people are skeptical that it will ever get started because we have had so many starts in the past. However, it now appears that it will go ahead. To say the least, we are excited. Our business communities have come together to make sure that we have the best possible facilities to address the needs of the people and the companies involved in building the project.

Government Orders
The project has met all the standards demanded by the environmental review process. It has met the standards of the P.E.I., New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and federal governments. It has passed the referendum process in Prince Edward Island. It is extremely important to people in the area. It is a win-win situation for everyone as we see it.
One member said it had a one-two punch a little while ago. I would like to add a few more punches to it. He said it had one punch as a construction project, that is true, and a second punch as a tourist attraction.
Probably the most important punch is that it will be a key to our transportation infrastructure in Atlantic Canada. It will be a very integral part of the over-all transportation system and it will help us as a region to be competitive, and help Prince Edward Island specifically to be competitive.
Certainly the over-all economic impact will be substantial. We have heard figures today of $800 million and $850 million, and we have heard figures even higher than that. By the time it is done the peripheral impact and all the housing, supplies, and services and goods that must be supplied to the people will be over $1 billion. That is very attractive to us in our area.
The people of the region are most excited and anxious to see it go ahead. I appreciate this opportunity to speak on it and I certainly hope it moves along as quickly as possible and is as successful as we think it will be.

Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker in his remarks referred a number of times to environmental assessment and said that the project has undergone a number of environmental assessments.
That is true. The environmental assessment recommended that the project not proceed. How does he justify supporting a bill that the project proceed when the environmental assessment said no?

Mr. Speaker, the environmental assessment said the project should not proceed if the ice-out was going to be a seven days delay as it predicted.
When the specific environmental assessment on the ice-out was done this generic plan came up with the criteria that it would only limit the ice to two days a year.
The original reason for recommending it not proceed was that the environmental assessment panel predicted that it would take seven days for the ice to go out. That was just an assessment, and based on that assessment it should not go ahead. However, the panel said if it could meet a two-day ice-out it could go ahead. The present plan more than meets that criteria.

all their time talking about there not being enough money for the unemployed, for unemployment insurance and no new money to create out there off the so-called money tree for projects. We hear every single day from the Tories and from the Minister of Finance about how they are responsible for fiscal matters of this country. My dear friends over here, be serious. How serious can you be if you are so dumb as to spend $42 million a year to save $21 million a year? Do you think I am exaggerating? the years and what do they say to me? "Oh, you're going to lose votes in P.E.I." If they want to buy votes, they can do it a hell of a lot better and a lot cheaper than this kind of buy-out. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext: You are picking on little Prince Edward Island.

Picking on Prince Edward Island? Its people think it is a joke. They think it is a great deal of fun to pull the wool over Canadian eyes, saying we can spend $42 million a year to save $21 million a year. This is the new Tory-Liberal thinking.
I challenge the members from New Brunswick and P.E.I. to stand up on the platform and say: "This is the way we are going to get this country out of the financial mess. That is the absolute reality. How do they justify the Great Britain and United States company's 70 per cent consortium owned offshore? Why are we spending the money to enhance contractors in Great Britain? I do not know. Why are we spending the money to enhance contractors in the United States? I do not know.

February 22, 1993
Government Orders
I want to let you in on a secret. I know this project is dumb. I know there are politics involved and I know they are seeking votes, but there are no votes for this government in England. Those members have not even figured that out. There are no votes for this government in the United States. They have not figured that out either.
If you are going to sell out, if you are going to do something for political reasons, at least do it where you will get some votes. You are insulting the integrity of the traditional honour of buying votes by going offshore. You are buying votes in Britain and the United States. That is dumb.
Now for the Liberals, why are they agreeing with this? Do they think they are going to get votes out of it? They already have seats in P.E.I. What are they going to get out of it? Are they going to say: "Look at us. We have an edifice complex. We helped build this bridge. We can have our name on a bronze plaque" right at the level where the sea salt water will erode the quickest, we hope.
There will be all the sitting members of Parliament cemented into this bridge. There they are for posterity, every one of them. Do you know what? They are hoping that everybody in P.E.I. will come, look at their names on the bridge and say: "Mmm, I am going to vote for that guy".
They are insulting the people of P.E.I. They are insulting the people of New Brunswick and they are insulting the rest of us Canadians. I thought this kind of pork-barrel politics was over.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext: What do you suggest?

I suggest that if you can find an extra $21 million a year, you can start spending on people who are hungry.
Spend it on kids who can go to school and have a hot meal inside their stomachs. Spend it on the education of people in P.E.I. Spend $42 million a year on university and technical schools in the maritimes. Upgrade those schools that you blab about over there all the time.
Spend money for the seniors. Spend money for the pioneers who built this country, but not $42 million a year to provide some offshore corporations with money that they can profit from to save $21 million a year.
What do I suggest? I will tell you what I suggest. Your mathematics are stupid. The project does not make sense. Also, anybody who gets up in this House and supports it by saying: "We can solve a $21 million a year problem by spending $42 million" needs their head examined by the Auditor General.
I challenge this government and the opposition to call in the Auditor General and have him do a study of this. I challenge them to say the Auditor General can show how you can save $21 million a year by spending $42 million a year.
It is the same kind of mentality as spending all that money on Hibernia to provide the Americans with offshore oil. Even the ships and the infrastructure for Hibernia are being built offshore. I do not understand it. If it is good politics, then let the people of New Brunswick and Newfoundland decide if they want the money directly in their pockets. Do they think it should be diverted through the consortium that is owned in Britain and the United States?
What are the economic impact studies? Who has done them? What of the environmental studies? Many more need to be done. What about the way of life on Prince Edward Island being the same as British Columbia? We have Vancouver Island. Do you want to spend $45 million a year to solve our ferry problems? You have not given the province of British Columbia one single penny to pay for transportation between the mainland and Victoria, not one penny.
Since W.A.C. Bennett brought in the ferry system between Vancouver Island and the mainland, not one cent of Canadian taxpayers' dollars has gone to help British Columbia's need for intercoastal ferries, not one penny. Those ferries are built in B.C. by B.C. workers in union shops. They are not on strike.
I am not here to lament the failures of past Liberal and Tory governments. I want to put that on record but how can you keep that up and deny the rest of the Canadian people an option for the same money? Is it politics? It is stupidity, absolute stupidity.
I challenge every single Tory cabinet minister who holds a seat from Manitoba west to come on a public platform with me and justify this project financially in western Canada.
February 22, 1993

I challenge the cabinet ministers from the province of British Columbia to have a public meeting in Vancouver, stand up on a platform and say: "Yes, we have decided on a new way to save money. We are going to spend $42 million a year to save $21 million in P.E.I. and you still do not get a penny out here in British Columbia".
Since 1960 we have built and run government owned ferries in the province of British Columbia, paid for by the taxpayers of British Columbia and not one cent came from Ottawa. We never once complained about the subsidies given to the maritimes. Now we are complaining that the subsidies are misdirected.
And they took away the Polar 8.

The Polar 8. We never even got that.
I agree with those critics but my agreement is something more uncomplicated. This is sheer vote buying at the stupidest level that one can think. If you want to do some vote buying, give the money directly to the people, not to a consortium offshore and not for a fixed link that makes up for the missing link that does not go with the thinking both of the Liberals and of the Tories.
You cannot justify this financially. You should all be ashamed of yourselves in supporting this, every single one of you.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca who commented about insulting the people of Prince Edward Island that the majority of people in Prince Edward Island voted for the fixed link to New Brunswick.
We have heard the NDP with its high moral pronouncements for some time now. The previous speaker just alluded to what a thin veneer that actually is.

Mr. Speaker, if this gentleman is saying this is not to buy votes in P.E.I., if the hon. gentleman is saying that four seats do not count, let me remind the member that politicians count every single seat as important. He did not address the specific problem that I raised. Why spend $42 million a year to solve a $21 million a year problem? You are a Liberal and you support it. speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Solicitor General of Canada):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was driven to my feet by the logic of my hon. friend.
For years the province of British Columbia has argued that the Government of Canada should run a railroad train up and down Vancouver Island on the basis that it was in the original agreement whereby B.C. came into Confederation.
My hon. friend should obviously know that in the original agreement whereby P.E.I. came into Confederation it was guaranteed access to the mainland. What we are trying to do is give them better access, access that does not break down.
My hon. friend is not from the province of Ontario where we have tourists going to P.E.I. all the time. The biggest problem is the wait for the ferry. My hon. friend does not know anything about that. In your party you maybe do not have to wait for ferries but in our party you do.
You can wait for hours in B.C.
I think my hon. friend has to get it right. If he wants to apply the principle when it comes to B.C. he has got to apply the principle when it comes to P.E.I.
Do you think that the Tories recognized the principle of the E & N railroad when CPR closed it down?
No.

No. We had to go to court. We did not get any help from the federal government. You are the ones that allowed the railroads to be disbanded. The passenger service that was promised when the CPR came in, it was the Liberals and the Tories that took the CPR off the hook, and never took back one single Crown grant. They gave them forest rights, they gave them mineral rights in this country, they gave them land 10 miles on both sides of the railroads and as soon as the railroad said "Oh, we are going broke" the government said "We cannot stand this. You poor railroads. We will take it over and pay for it out of taxpayers money".
Do not give me that humbug that this government or the Liberals ever stood up for the Canadian people on the original deal on the railroads. We had to go to the Supreme Court of British Columbia to get our rights to get the railroad back.
The record of both the Liberals and the Conservatives is one of consistent sell out, not only of the west but every single taxpayer in this country. To suggest that there is any difference between this government and the Liberals is absolutely a fabrication. The people of this country are getting hosed again by stupid deals that do not even have a reasonable payout to ordinary people in this country.
I cannot make it plainer than that. I challenge my good friends to stand up on any public platform in any city of this country and argue this stupidity. I will argue against it and we will see what the audience thinks.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Barbara Sparrow (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased as an Albertan to be able to participate in the debate on Bill C-110. I have to say I was quite appalled at the previous speaker with regard to how Canada works together to help its brothers and sisters from coast to coast.
This bill takes us into the future. We are not going to continue to live in the past. We are going to move forward so we can be more competitive and give the people in the Atlantic region of Canada the ability to have upgraded infrastructure to promote their agriculture and their tourism and allow them to get on with things that you and I, Mr. Speaker, take for granted because they have been in our provinces for quite some time.
The positive economic factors of this bill are far greater than any of the negatives my friend from Esquimau has been talking about. As a matter of fact it is probably one of the greatest opportunities that P.E.I. has ever had. I congratulate P.E.I. and its former premier, Joe Ghiz, as well as the former premier of New Brunswick, who worked very diligently and hard with the federal government to see this come to a reality.
I have had two or three questions with regard to the environmental review. I have to say that environmental reviews are very important with regard to all projects. This one was submitted to an environmental review. There were certain qualifications put on it with regard to the ice flow. With all due respect the government did appoint a very special committee of ice experts who said that if a bridge or the fixed link could be built with less than two days ice-out per year it would be all right with EARP or the Environmental Assessment Review Panel, which of course was done.
Let us just back up a bit and talk about this. This is not something new. It has been going on now for pretty well seven years and has been through the various environmental studies. I have to say that a plebiscite was held in

February 22, 1993
Government Orders
P.E.I., I believe in 1988, and the majority of people on the Island voted in favour of the fixed link.
We all recognize there were some who voted against it for various reasons. A lot of them would have to do with their feeling of becoming too modem or taking them into the next century where they do not want to move. It was a fair vote. It did win the majority and we will go ahead with it. As I said, the ice flow has been taken care of which then means that the environmental review does stand approved.
With regard to the subsidy of $21 million the hon. member from B.C. discussed a few minutes ago, every year it costs to operate ferries between New Brunswick and P.E.I., something in the area of $21 million or $22 million.
It was $27 million in 1988.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
In 1988 it was $27 million. We also have a problem with regard to the age of the ferries and the mechanical upkeep and repair that need to be done. There have been proven documents set forth with regard to the need for four as a minimum and perhaps five new ferries. Each new ferry would cost between $110 million and $140 million. If that is prorated with the operating costs and the capital expenditures over the 35 years then we come to the $42 million in 1992 dollars. It is not a gift of the taxpayers of Canada. Indeed we are building the capital expenditures into the operating expenditures and putting out some pure facts.
I want to speak a bit about the call for proposals. Three proposals were accepted. On the final review the winning firm was Strait Crossing Incorporated with its head office in the city of Calgary from whence I come. While it is a consortium, it is a Canadian company with its head office there. Not 100 per cent but 95 per cent of the work is going to be Canadian content, with most of it coming from the Atlantic coast, which is right. Of course the engineering and design of the fixed link will be done in Calgary.
It is a private sector responsibility. The private sector designs it. The private sector engineers it. The private sector finances it. It is constructed by the private sector. It is operated by the private sector for 35 years, after which time it will revert to the government. It is all private sector.
In these specific issues the private sector assumes all the risk and the government subsidy or the $42 million is what we would pay annually anyway over a prorated 35 years. It is environmentally sound. It met the ice review committee recommendations. There will be less than two ice-outs a year. It will bring a lot of regional benefits to P.E.I., to New Brunswick and to the Nova Scotia area.
Built into the costs will be the toll rates. We will utilize the costs of the fixed link when it is completed. The toll rate will be based on the ferry crossing, increased with a CPI or an inflationary indexation period. That is all laid down specifically in the contracts.
Strait Crossing Inc., the company from Calgary, has also built in costs with regard to constant maintenance and constant upkeep so that we do not run into difficulties 10, 20, 30 or 40 years down the road, which certainly could happen. However these are the built-in costs that will be paid by the toll rates that will be instituted when the bridge is completed.
Also a performance bond has been posted by Strait Crossing Inc. and there is insurance with regard to the fisheries. It was quite interesting to hear some of my colleagues on the other side of the House worry about any negative effect it could have on the fishing industry, which of course as we all know is a major industry for P.E.I., as well as for other areas.
If we take a look at the offshore rigs down on the gulf coast or where there has been offshore activity with different types of industry, it is surprising to see how the fishing industries have not really been hurt in any way. It has been very positive with regard to the habitat and the increase in availability of the product. There is not any factual evidence showing that there will be hurt or damage done to that particular industry, but there has been a bond posted in case of a problem.
I have to say with regard to selecting the company in Calgary that this gives benefits right across the country. There will be designers and engineers in Calgary who would be working on this issue. There is a range of products and services.
There is the supplying of the cement which will probably come mainly from the Atlantic provinces and the aggregates of steel. There is the selling and leasing of the heavy equipment. There is the construction of
February 22, 1993

roads and the facilities for the on and off ramps. There is a whole variety of other services that will come out of P.E.I. or New Brunswick. Some of these smaller local businesses in existence in Atlantic Canada will forge ahead. The response we have had from industries in P.E.I., which will be producing most of the work has been extremely positive.
One of the key requirements for the project is that the developer maximize the use of Atlantic Canada. Why not? This should benefit those people. SCI is currently preparing an industrial benefits plan which is to be submitted to the government. I know my colleague in the NDP will be interested that SCI is currently producing an industrial benefits plan that has to be submitted to the government, and indeed the Minister of Public Works, and has to meet certain criteria that have been set down before the federal government will give its final approval to sign the contract and move ahead.
There are jobs for P.E.I. There are benefits for P.E.I., New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, as well as the western provinces. This is part of building Canada. This is when the east helps the west or vice versa. This is part of how our country was built in the very beginning. Those who have a bit more than the others share. This represents not only an economic move forward for P.E.I., but it shows what Canadians can do right across the country.
Turning to the operating period, once the fixed link is up and operating what are the tolls? The tolls will be based on the cost of the ferry crossings, as I said, increased with the CPI or the inflation rate. There will be an agreed upon amount of capital for the repairs and maintenance of the plan. That is to be independently reviewed outside government to make sure that it meets the criteria set down. There is to be no payment made to the developer until all the criteria are outlined and have been proven.
What is most interesting is to see colleagues, one might say from both sides of the House, who appear to agree on something that is so necessary to move P.E.I. into the 21st century. It also brings P.E.I. up to some of the increased trading arrangements.
When I look to the agriculture area, as well as the fishing area and tourism, I think that P.E.I. certainly deserves all this. Indeed, we will be watching very
Government Orders
carefully as we go through the years waiting for the bridge to be opened.
As a member of the House on the government side from the province of Alberta I truly support this bill. It brings Canadians together. It moves us forward. We are not going to sit and keep looking at the past. This is where everybody can work together to make this country work.

Mr. Speaker, I have received some criticism from people in Prince Edward Island who do not take kindly to a member from British Columbia "interfering with their business".
I take exception to that analysis of this. I am an islander. I see this as a union of islanders. The fishermen and the ferry workers on Prince Edward Island, the friends of the island, consider that I am speaking out for them. It is certainly not their Liberal representatives who are speaking out for them.
I also think it is my duty as a member of Parliament. When $42 million a year is going to be expended on a project, I am not interfering. I am doing my job in criticizing that project. I am also doing my job when the environmental assessment integrity process is so sullied by this government in putting forth this idea. That is doing my job as a member of Parliament.
What we have seen is that the Liberals and the government are prepared to put forward a bill which they think will guarantee their votes in the maritimes. As a member from British Columbia, a member from an island, I have a duty to respond and a duty to speak out against this project.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like each and every one of us the hon. member was elected by the constituents in her riding. She certainly has the right to speak of their views and their wishes within this particular House. I would hope that while she does that she takes the views of all of Canada because when we come here as elected members we are representing Canada as a whole.
While it is very important to know the views and concerns of her local constituents and make sure that they are heard, a lot of the decisions we make here have to reflect all of Canada. Some parts of Canada are more blessed with certain resources than other areas. Since the beginning, long before 1867, it has been part of the Canadian way to help each other.

Government Orders
I have no problem with the member expressing the views and concerns of her people. However, I also hope the member realizes she is here representing not only her constituents from the island of Vancouver but she is also here making decisions for all of Canada.
It is very important that the hon. member look at the people of P.E.I. as well as the people of New Brunswick. Allow them the infrastructure for them to get ahead and promote their industry, be it fisheries, tourism, forestry, potatoes or agriculture.
I think it is incumbent upon the hon. member to speak for all of Canada as well as her own specific constituents.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of my friend. Not too long ago in this House we listened to the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. I for one would love to be his speech-writer because he only said three things. It would not take me too long to write that.
One of the things he said was that the rest of the members who are in favour of this particular piece of legislation obviously are stupid. We are not intelligent enough to be able to see the writing on the wall. He also said that we must be trying to buy votes.
The only piece of information he gave us throughout the whole speech, which I found quite interesting, is that at present it costs roughly $21 million to transport people back and forth between the island and the mainland and it would cost roughly $42 million a year throughout the whole cost of the project and the continuous time it would take to pay it off.
What he failed to mention should be brought forward in the House. I would like to ask the hon. member if she could elaborate on this. What are some of the other economic development spin-offs created by these kinds of projects, which when added is a cost factor in itself, would help the islanders with better access to the mainland and entice businesses to want to move to the island because of the guaranteed access?
It is important for us to put some of those different issues on the record. Therefore, we do not give the impression the only thing we are doing is being stupid
and buying votes but that we do have some understanding of the economics of this issue.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question and the comments from my colleague.
With regard to the $42 million a year in subsidy for the 35 years, that includes both the operating and capital expenditures.
The previous member of the New Democratic Party from Esquimalt kept harping on $21 million, $22 million plus a giveaway of another $21 million of taxpayers' money. This is not true. When operating ferries there are operating costs and capital costs. There is repair and maintenance every year and every once in a while a feny has to be replaced. So what is built into the 35 years on the $42 million subsidy each year is capital costs as well as the operating cost. It is very fair and legitimate.
Second, it was said the project did not meet the EARP, the Environmental Assessment Review Panel. It did. There were certain ice-out conditions that the EARP panel brought forward. These were reviewed and certain criteria were set down by the special ice committee that was formed. The winning contractor has indeed met the specific criteria.
The infrastructure for P.E.I. is extremely important. It is for every city and every province, but specifically in the Atlantic and in P.E.I. We deal mainly with the agriculture and fisheries industries of which time and weather plays a main role. In order to get the product to market fresh and quickly obviously a fixed link, which is 100 per cent reliable, is the best way to go.
I believe tourism is the second major industry for the province of Prince Edward Island. People can come and go at their own time. They can cross over or cross back when they want to. It makes it a lot easier.
With regard to improving the infrastructure and the highway systems on both sides, be it in New Brunswick or in P.E.I., this has been taken into consideration. In fact it met one of the 10 proposals the former premier of P.E.I. set down before he would sign the particular proposal.
Sure we are building infrastructure. We are taking it into the next century. It is going to make P.E.I., New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and indeed Newfoundland, more competitive. Is that not what this country is all about?
February 22, 1993

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member talked about the support among the fishing community for the fixed link. However, she will know that on February 6 at its annual general meeting the P.E.I. Fishermen's Association voted unanimously against the link. In fact it argued that a full environmental review should take place to assess the environmental consequences of the fixed link.
I wonder whether as a result of the unanimous opposition by P.E.I. fishermen the member would care to rethink her indications that there is so much support across Prince Edward Island for this link.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fishing industry certainly has been taken into very serious consideration because it is a major industry for the island. We recognize that.
Looking at other places throughout the globe where there has been activity, be it construction or engineering, in the areas where there is a very prolific fishing industry indeed it can be seen that it can be more of a benefit than a negative.
Also built into the trust fund by Strait Crossing Inc. is a $10 million fund specifically for the fishing industry. It is not that we are taking this lightly. We are taking it extremely seriously. None of these things have been overlooked. Therefore rest assured that fishing is a major industry and has been taken into consideration.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
Pursuant to Standing Order 83(2), I would like you to designate an Order of the Day to consider the notice of Ways and Means motion tabled earlier today.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to participate in this debate today.
Unfortunately earlier we got into sort of a regional debate between east and west. Having practised law in the west and having children in the west and being a member from the east, I bring a very real Canadian perspective to this.
I am from the east. I am a maritimer, an Atlantic Canadian and a member from Nova Scotia. I want to declare my bias right at the start that philosophically I am against a fixed link to P.E.I. That is my philosophy.
Government Orders
Knowing a little about Atlantic Canada and P.E.I. I fundamentally believe that a fixed link will change the character of the island. Those who think this is going to be such a boon to the island are very misguided.
The boom-and there is going to be a boon and a boom-is that obviously jobs are going to occur on the mainland. Amherst, Moncton, the mainland area is going to perhaps develop beyond the construction jobs. That is where some of the suboffices are going to be. You will be able to scoot on to the island over the bridge. You will be able to drive on and off all within a day.
This could be such a fundamental shift in the whole social order of the island that the fabled Anne of Green Gables is going to become the witch of Cavendish. She very well could because of the change that will occur.
I have declared my bias. What a lot of people are missing, sincerely, I believe-we always sincerely debate in this Chamber even though we sometimes get a little political. What a lot of people are missing is that the environmental panel created by the federal government legislation assessed all the impacts, both plus and minus.
The plebiscite on the island was not for the bridge that this bill is for. It was for the vague term fixed link. It could be a bridge or it could be a tunnel. The environmental study finally was concluded and was referred to before. It was the Northumberland Strait Crossing Project report of the environment assessment panel dated August 1990.
It reviewed all the pluses and minuses and then came out and said: "The panel agrees that there is a need for an improved transportation service between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. After careful consideration, however, the panel concludes that the risk of harmful effects of the proposed bridge concept is unacceptable. The panel recommends therefore that the project not proceed".
This is the latest in the federal environmental panel. Subsequent to that there was a subsidiary ice panel that is not under the federal act which did the total survey.
The federal environmental panel itself says that improved access is needed. I am all for improved access to P.E.I. However the bridge was not approved.

February 22, 1993
Government Orders
In the summary it says: "The panel concludes that subject to a favourable independent environmental review a tunnel concept might be an acceptable transportation link between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. The panel further concludes that an improved ferry service might also be acceptable".
A bridge is not the only alternative to improve access to the island to maintain the constitutional necessity of a link to Canada. This is what is being lost in this drive to start this project.
Mr. Speaker, you are too young in the chair, and some of the members of the House are too young in the chair to remember but the concept of a fixed link with the island in the east is as old as the Chignecto canal. It is as old as linking the Fundy tides that could provide renewable power in an awesome way.
We have been through all that. I think the former member for Moncton and the mother of the present member for Moncton has a golden shovel in her basement for digging some of the foundation for the causeway back in 1966. We can actually still see some of the roadwork and/or the mudwork of what was going to be a causeway.
My point in saying no to this bill is that even though it takes time the study should be complete. I know there have been hundreds of studies but not in this modem age of technology. In effect the federal government's own environmental panel said no to the bridge and said it is for some of the alternatives. My philosophical bias is against a link. I am not an islander but I love the island. I think an awful lot of people come to that island because it is the way it is. A fixed link, especially the bridge, is fundamentally going to change it.
I have tried to be easy on this because obviously as an Atlantic Canadian, as a maritimer, I want to see jobs in an area that is in dire straits in so many ways. Obviously anything that can help in the construction itself is going to be a pump-primer. It may be for political purposes, and that is not unreal and certainly a surprise. Perhaps that is the reason we are trying to move the thing along.
I really tried to be as rational as I could. I tried to give the benefit of the doubt, to take care of my bias, and determine if the project, the fixed link and/or the bridge, will be financially and economically feasible.
This is the other general objection. I admit my bias but I am trying to resolve my bias. What I fundamentally criticize the present government for is not coming clean. My objection to this bill would not be so fundamental and I might even go along with it to get it into committee if the government came clean and did not pretend it was going to cost only $800 million when we all know it is going to cost much more.
I only have to look at the most meaningful study that was commissioned on the fixed link and the bridge by Woods Gordon in 1987. It estimated that the bridge would cost $1.3 billion, not the $800 million that the minister talked about when he introduced this bill on February 8. If that was the estimate in 1987 just imagine what the estimate is today. If members who vote for this bill are honest with their taxpayer constituents-this place is in such disrepute because we try to play with figures and smoke and mirrors. How can anyone say the bridge will only cost $800 million? That is the figure I looked up while I was waiting to be recognized by Your Honour. On February 8 the minister said $800 million and that is in the press release.
The parliamentary secretary today said $850 million. What is $800 million or $850 million? That is a long way, millions, hundreds of millions, from the $1.3 billion estimate in 1987.
Members in favour of this bill should admit that it is not going to be $800 million; it is going to be $1.5 billion. It was $1.3 billion in 1987. Let us use our common sense. Let us look at another crossing linking mainland with an island, the chunnel in Europe from France to England.
Is it not interesting that in 1987 the estimate for the chunnel, that is the tunnel, was $9 billion? Yet, in actual fact today the cost is already $16 billion. That is private enterprise. It is not supposed to involve taxpayers' money. They are having some real difficulties because of contractor fights, and I do not have time to get into that.
The point is that a $9 billion estimate in 1987 has become a $16 billion cost today with overruns along the way. Who believes that the $1.3 billion estimate of
February 22, 1993

Woods Gordon in 1987 will not grow in like fashion to not the $1.3 billion suggested in 1987 but closer to $2 billion if this thing ever goes ahead?
The other area in which there is a lot of misinformation is-and the hon. member for Calgary Southwest touched on it. The member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca made one of his typical and very bombastic contributions to this debate. It certainly was very interesting but I do not know how much light it shed. We can play with the figure of a $42 million subsidy a year for 35 years and say that is balanced against a $21 million subsidy that is actually paid to the ferries, and some years it is $21 million. However, the evidence really is that Marine Atlantic estimates that, using capital and operating costs that the member for Calgary Southwest mentioned, the figure for subsidy amortized over the 35-year period is $29.5 million. In other words, it is $30 million.
Let us assume that its figures are correct. We should not use the $21 million that is sometimes the subsidy in some years. Marine Atlantic has been great, the subsidy has been coming down and $21 million to $22 million has been the figure for the last few years. Using operating and capital costs and Marine Atlantic's own figures we get up to $29.5 million, or let us call it $30 million. Even $30 million is still $12 million less than the $42 million figure. There is an extra payment to help private enterprise of over $400 million.
There must be some frankness and openness here. Let the members who support this bill admit that the estimate is woefully low, that in 1987 figures it was $1.3 billion and it is going to be even more six years later. Let them admit that there is taxpayer money in this, that it is $42 million for 35 years, of which at least $12 million is extra and above whatever the subsidy is, so there is going to be a cost.
What happens at the end? After 35 years, after it has been built and run by the consortium, it is then given back to the Canadian taxpayer. I am not an engineer. However I certainly know about Lions Gate Bridge in Vancouver, British Columbia. Other colleagues have perhaps other ideas and knowledge about other bridges. A bridge over salt water, not to mention the salt that drips off the vehicles that are going to drive across it, has horrendous maintenance problems. While the life of the form of the bridge may be 100 years in Parliaments ahead when we are long gone the maintenance costs on an
Government Orders
annual basis will be very close to the subsidy that is presently being given to the ferry.
That is something that should be considered as members consider this bill.
This bridge is almost like a Trojan Horse. There are a lot of nice things about it. It is going to create jobs. It is going to speed up some traffic. Let us take it in like the people of Troy did before their city crumbled. This is not a Trojan Horse but it is going to be a Trojan bridge. There are a lot of deceptive things that come with this bridge that will not do all the good things that many of the speakers here in this House, in their honest belief, have said it will.
Something that I am very concerned with, and that no one has touched on concerning this link to expedite traffic back and forth, is how the bridge is going to operate. It is very interesting that in all the studies done on the subject only part deals with how this bridge is going to operate.
The Department of Public Works has a document entitled Investigation Into the Effect of Wind on Vehicular Traffic. There are some pretty sobering statistics in it as to how fast people are going to go across that bridge in view of the wind on the Strait, compared to even waiting for the ferries.
The Public Works document points out that due to the height of the bridge-63 metres or around 200 feet at its highest point-and the fact that it is over a large body of water where strong winds prevail much of the time: "At 50 metres winds of 40 kilometres will occur 84 per cent of the time; winds between 40 and 50 kilometres will force traffic to slow down to 40 kilometres, extending crossing time from 13 to 22 minutes. As winds increase from 50 to 70 kilometres more drastic measures are required, including conveying empty trucks at low speed thus slowing all traffic. Winds over 50 kilometres exist over 40 per cent of the time. Winds of 70 to 100 kilometres will see traffic slow to 30 kilometres, and empty trucks will not be permitted to cross until the winds die down. Winds over 100 kilometres will see all cars conveyed at 20 kilometres, taking 39 minutes, or conversely the bridge could be shut down".
The time that has been mentioned in this debate so far about the expeditious crossing because of a bridge, 13 minutes, is only for ideal conditions. When the winds get over 50 kilometres, which is over half the time, then traffic starts to build up behind as cars funnel onto the

February 22, 1993
Government Orders
bridge. It is not going to be quite the whizzing over and getting off, even though it is obviously a little more permanent than a ferry boat.
I believe the member for Egmont would know, but I think the ferry was only really closed down-I admit it has been delayed-about five days a year on average. I do not know if it is even five days but that is roughly the figure. Obviously people do have to wait in the summertime. The member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca pointed out that people also have to wait for ferries in British Columbia to get to Vancouver Island; two or three sailings sometimes.
In any event, that is where the notion of the Trojan Horse comes into the picture. After all the debate up and down, and it is a mammoth structure, no one really knows just how much that wind over the ice pack and the Strait is going to slow down traffic.
I have tried to be reasonable and get other justifications for it. In my own hometown there is a professor of economics who is an expert on large megaprojects. He has done a study on the bridge and did a study of the Public Works study which was the justification for proceeding with the bridge. That was the Fiander-Good study of 1987.
Professor Townley, at Acadia, questions the very fundamentals of the economics of the bridge. He argues that one of the main economic feasibility studies done for Public Works by Fiander-Good in 1987 was seriously flawed. He says, among other things, that: "The economic feasibility of the fixed link has not been established". Further he says that: "Construction of a fixed link would impose a net loss on society. From this perspective a debate concerning the magnitude of any ensuing environmental damage would seem moot. Any damage at all would simply magnify this social loss". That is what Professor Townley says on page 18 of his article called "The Weakest Link" in Policy Options of July-August 1992.
Let me mention that because of Professor Townley's article there was another economic study commissioned to look into the economic feasibility of the bridge. Just recently another group has come out supporting his conclusions. I believe as a mainlander that the social order of P.E.I. will be fundamentally changed in a negative way, when it is all shaken out, which very well
may have some negative impacts on the tourism industry that attracts people there by the droves in the summertime. Anne of Green Gables is going to become the witch of Cavendish if we do not watch out. We cannot really fully assess that. Then we look at some of the outside facts-starting with the environmental panel study that is fundamental if we believe in our own laws. You do that and it says not to go ahead. It says canvass some other alternatives and they have not been canvassed. Then you look at the fake figure of $800 million being used by the minister. Yet in 1987, six years ago, the figure was $1.3 billion. Compare that to what happened to the chunnel in 1987. It went from $9 billion to $16 billion. You are going to have the same ratio of increase. Then there is this figure you really can play with, the $42 million per year of subsidy.
In conclusion, because I know my time is just about up, on the $42 million I said you could be very reasonable. You cannot deny that $29.5 million or $30 million is the amortized subsidy. Therefore it is a $12 million difference. Politically and not getting into the buying of votes, what concerns me seriously as an Atlantic Canadian along with other Canadians, be they from British Columbia or elsewhere across the country who have been kind and good to Atlantic Canada, an area of regional and economic disparity, if I were just an ordinary taxpayer tuning on the television national news or prime time or whatever it is called now and saw that at this time of financial restraint when we are all supposed to be tightening our belts that the Government of Canada was proceeding with a fixed link that has been talked about since Confederation and proceeding against some of these reports, I as a taxpayer would have difficulty believing other things the government has said. To me in terms of Atlantic Canada which needs Canadian help it is something we should consider before we go any further with this.

Mr. Speaker, the fixed link crossing to P.E.I. is something we have talked about over the past number of years. In fact, when we look at the province of Prince Edward Island and how it came into Confederation, it was predicated on that promise of assured linkage. We have gone from the steamers that originally crossed between P.E.I. and the mainland, the province of New Brunswick, and now we have resurrected the question of a fixed link. As I have
February 22, 1993

alluded to, it is not the first time we have discussed this in the House. It had been discussed long before I arrived.
Hopefully we have come up with a plan that will work and one that I think most of us can accept once we have a chance to go through the numbers and find out what we presently have, what we are going to propose and whether or not it is a real alternative.
I will start by mentioning that in my riding of Carle-ton-Charlotte, there are three islands in the Bay of Fundy. As any member who has islands in their riding knows, it is quite difficult most of the time to visit them as frequently as you would like. Of those three islands I have Campobello Island, Deer Island and Grand Manan Island. One of those does have a fixed link now. Campobello Island is linked actually to mainland United States. Indeed, if you are a Canadian travelling to Campobello and you want to get there by automobile you have to travel through the continental United States to get there.
I can remember when that bridge was being built. It was something like the debate we are carrying on here today in the House of Commons. There are some interesting parallels between the debate to build a bridge to Campobello Island 30 years ago and the debate we are having here today. At that time there was mixed opinion as to whether there should be a bridge to Campobello Island. Of course, some of the arguments and some of the things we are hearing here today were suggested back then, such as the impact it would have on the fisheries and whether we could engineer a bridge to Campobello Island. But it was built. As I said, there was controversy at the time as to whether or not the people would accept it.
At the time, going back 30 years, I was just a very young boy, but I can remember there were some pretty strong arguments against it. At the end of the day, obviously the strong arguments for it won out.
It is interesting to note that the member of Parliament at the time who supported the construction of the bridge was defeated in the next election. Maybe the opposition members will take some comfort in that. It was a very emotional project at the time. If you visit the island of
Government Orders
Campobello today, you will find that the people of that island support it to the tune of 95 to 100 per cent. It has been good and necessary for the island.
When we look at P.E.I., they are going through somewhat the same debate today. One of the things that was done in P.E.I. was to seek support from native islanders as to whether it was something they desired. Most of us accept the level of support given on the island for a fixed link. If my memory serves me correctly, 60 per cent of the islanders are in favour of a fixed link.
The argument in regard to cost is interesting. I believe that some members in the House are not putting forward an intellectually honest argument in the sense that there will be a burden of cost on the federal government if we proceed with the project. That has to be cleared up because indeed there is a cost to the Government of Canada today. When I talk about the Government of Canada , of course I am talking about the taxpayers. As we know, these are the people who really pay the bills.
Today there is a cost of maintaining that linkage to the mainland with the ferries. That amounts to about $27.5 million per year every year. That is the annual subsidy to maintain that link today but it is not the total cost. The total cost has to consider such things as the replacement ferries. As we all know in this House, any time you are operating a boat or a ferry, at some point you have to replace it.
We are told that the replacement cost on those ferries, and the member next to me can clarify this because I know that he has done some research on that, is in the order of $50 million in the next number of years.
$500 million.
Five hundred million dollars. It is $50 million per vessel.
For half a vessel.

For half a vessel. So he is saying $100 million per vessel.
This means a $500 million replacement cost, half a billion dollars. There is indeed an added expense at the end of the day when the present vessels get to the end of their life span. They are very close to that now.

Government Orders
There is one point I wish to pick up on, and I know that the minister of fisheries mentioned this in relation to some questions from the other side of the House coming from the member from British Columbia.
This is a project that normally the opposition would be screaming for. How many times in this House have we heard the opposition talking about putting money into infrastructure? How many times? We have heard it many times in this House, talk about kick-starting the economy. Let us get some public works projects off the ground and let us get this economy moving, particularly in Atlantic Canada.
That is exactly what this project is doing. If you wish, it is going to be a kick-start. I hate to use that word kick-start because it sounds as if you are just hooking jumper cables up to the economy and off it goes, as we often have to do with our automobiles here in the heart of winter. It is not quite that easy. Nonetheless, this project will be somewhere in the vicinity of $800 million. That is not an insignificant amount of money but it is going to be money that is raised through the private sector and put to work. It is not as if the Government of Canada is going to write a cheque for that $800 million. That is coming from the private sector, so it will be a project that will sustain itself.
The annual cost to the Government of Canada will not exceed the cost that we presently have today, $27.5 million, because there will be upkeep costs and other assorted costs in maintaining a structure of that kind.
I cannot understand the opposition members' argument or opposition to this project because they want megaprojects, they want money injected into local economies and particularly the poorer parts of Canada. This is a big project. It is one I do not think they should fly in the face of.
Again it is moneys being put up by the private sector, not the Government of Canada. It is important to lay that out veiy squarely. Our costs will not exceed the fixed costs that we presently have to maintain the ferry service.
The other argument I think is a very unfair one. As I mentioned before, the fisheries minister did speak on this and took up the clinical argument that this was a political project with a political agenda behind it, the re-election of Conservative members of Parliament.
We do not have any members of Parliament sitting on this side of the House from Prince Edward Island. I wish we did. There are some members from the other side that I see here today from the Liberal Party who represent that island. There are four seats on P.E.I., none of which government members hold. There is one vacancy there and maybe we will have a shot at it but we are not doing it for that reason.
You do not have a chance.

The member across is suggesting we do not have a chance at it. Maybe he is right, but time will tell. It is like a baseball game. You really cannot tell until it is over. Yogi Berra told us: "It's not over till its over".
That political argument is very shallow. I see the member over there nodding his head. He agrees it is a very shallow argument. We are doing the project and putting it together because it is the right thing to do for P.E.I. and it is the right thing to do for Atlantic Canada. We as New Brunswickers have a very keen interest in this project and want it to go ahead.
I want to step through about 10 points and these are key points that the P.E.I. government agreed to. It wanted it settled and agreement on it before it would agree to go ahead. I will go through those 10 points. I think I do have time.
The Ten Commandments.

The member from Nova Scotia is suggesting the Ten Commandments. The P.E.I. government was pretty rigid in these and we did give the government and the people of P.E.I. reassurance on each and every one of these.
One, an assurance that the P.E.I. highway system would have the capacity to handle the extra traffic that will be generated, and indeed there will be extra traffic generated. It should be a big boon for the island economy.
Two, an assurance that the Wood Island ferry service would be maintained. That has been given.
Three, the right to consult with the federal government on the establishment of tolls. That has been agreed to.
Four, fair treatment of displaced ferry workers-very important-including job training, relocation assistance and early retirement benefits because many of those workers are concerned and legitimately so, especially in
February 22, 1993

an economy where there are not a lot of options. That is something we have considered. It is nice to see that assurance has been given.
Five, the federal agreement to study further development opportunities for the Borden area to offset any negative effects of the project because their economy is based on that ferry run, or a degree of their economy.
Six, the assurance that the economic benefits to Atlantic Canada during the construction phase would be maximized. We all want to see that.
Seven, assurance that the project would meet the strict environmental criteria under the federal environmental assessment and review process. We are working in that regard.
Eight, compensation for fishermen whose livelihood may be adversely affected. That assurance has been given.
Nine, assurance that the fixed link will include a utility corridor at a reasonable cost to the province.
Ten, the Government of Prince Edward Island wished to ensure that the interests of its people were taken into full account before it would agree to proceed. It did agree to proceed in December. In December 1992 the province was satisfied that the conditions it had stipulated-those that I just outlined-had been met. As far as I am concerned they have been met and it will be a green light for this fixed project.
In conclusion, all I can say is that if they are going argue, and I do not think they are arguing too strenuously on the other side of the House, particularly those from Atlantic Canada, please argue on the basis of the project. Let us not float around some of these phoney numbers in regard to the cost to the federal government because there is no cost over and above the costs of maintaining those very ferries today.
I am proud to support this project. We would all like to see that it goes ahead.

Mr. Speaker, the member indicated he supports this bill. I wonder whether he has consulted with the Micmac people in New Brunswick as to their position on the fixed link
Government Orders
because I understand from my sources that they are not in favour of it.
I would also like to ask him if he is aware that the environmental assessment of the generic project recommended that the project not proceed. If he believes in the laws of Canada why does he now think that it is all right for the government to proceed?

Mr. Speaker, I have not had any correspondence with the Micmac people regarding this project. If the member does have correspondence and concerns raised by that particular group, if I could have a look at it I could understand the basis of her argument. However, I have not had any correspondence in that regard.
Concerning the environmental aspects, there is some misinformation with regard to the ice-out factor in the construction or the use of that facility. I think that has been clarified by the federal government and environmental experts who have looked at the project.
The record clearly indicates those considerations have been looked at. I do not believe it creates a problem that would jeopardize the structure at all. In fact the life of this structure-it is important that we put this on the record-as engineered is 100 years. It is important to state that because obviously it is a cost factor to be considered, the replacement of an existing bridge. Therefore, a 100-year life span is something that we can all take some comfort in, knowing it is not an expense which we will have to look at down the road in 25 or 30 years as some are suggesting.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate in this debate as a Canadian who supports efforts to ensure that weaker regions of the country have investment in their infrastructure and investment in their economies.
I also speak as a Canadian who spent 12 years living and working in the maritimes, and feel some appreciation of the particular problems of that region. I was in Prince Edward Island last week and among other things heard from ordinary citizens in Prince Edward Island of their opposition to the fixed link.
I am pleased to support the suggestion of my colleague, the member for Skeena, that rather than go ahead because of the ineffectual and faulty environmental assessment which has taken place, we refer this

Government Orders
matter to the Standing Committee on Environment so we can fully investigate the environmental implications of the link.
At least a couple of hoaxes are being perpetrated on some Canadians and on the people of Prince Edward Island. I will go into them in more detail afterwards but first of all, the government has said an effective environmental assessment review process has taken place when in fact that is not the case. To the extent that a environmental review by independent assessors has taken place the link has been shown to fall short of an appropriate environmental response.
Second, the hoax of the economics of the issue is being portrayed as advantageous and economically a good deal for Canada, a good deal for Prince Edward Island. The fixed link falls short on this basis too as I will relate.
The fixed link is being portrayed as being something that Prince Edward Islanders want. If we look at the question that was asked Prince Edward Islanders regarding the transportation issue between the island and the mainland, we will see that it is by no means clear that this fixed link is what Islanders chose.
We have, as we so often do, a situation where the Liberal members of Parliament, in this case from Prince Edward Island and from elsewhere, support a project proposed by the Conservative government. Both Liberals and Conservatives, two peas in a pod, are arguing the same points, ignoring the environmental implications of such an important project and the economic implications of such an important project. They are ignoring warnings from their own people in Prince Edward Island about the effects of the link.
My New Democratic Party colleagues and those whom I spoke with in Prince Edward Island last week are opposed to this plan for a fixed link because we are just talking here about a bridge. We are opposed because an appropriate environmental assessment review process was never carried out. We are opposed because the company which has the most interest in ensuring that this goes ahead, SCI, has really had phoney information sessions across the province to come up with the answers that it wanted in support of the link.
I want to speak a little about the issue itself, about the problems of the ferry service. Seven hundred ferry jobs are at stake. If we take the ferry away and if we add
others affected, perhaps 1,200 people will lose their jobs as a result of this project.
While there may be 1,000 or so jobs involved in building the fixed link, there will only be jobs while the link is being built. They will not be long-term jobs.
Many have asked questions about a better ferry service, an improved ferry service, rather than a fixed link. Across the world there are hydrofoils, hovercraft, as well as conventional ferries making fast, comfortable journeys for commercial and recreational purposes, making journeys further than those which are involved in Prince Edward Island. Somehow they get by without wasting billions of dollars on a bridge.
It is well recognized that the purchase of two additional ships would deal with the present problems of delays by those attempting to use the ferry service. Two new ferries would cost infinitely less, I think around $4 million, and would provide a service without the waiting for those going to and from the island. That is a far better investment than the over $1.5 billion which is being suggested for this link.
If we were really serious about dealing with the transportation issue on Prince Edward Island, we could solve it by providing a couple of extra ferries. We could save those 1,200 jobs and provide a service which would be satisfactory to those on the island.
I would like to go on to talk about the environmental impact. Clearly we would see increased environmental impact in a number of ways. If all those cars drove across on the fixed link, the environmental impact would be far greater than the impact of the ferries crossing over. That alone should be reason for concern.
The studies which have been done concerning the environment have given rise to serious concerns which have never been answered by the federal government except to the extent that the federal government has ignored them and set them aside. Never at any time did it provide extra information, facts or back-up for the arguments and the concerns raised by the environmental assessment which has taken place.
There are problems with ice being trapped and there are problems with the fishery. They cannot be ignored. It is not clear at all from the research which has been done
February 22, 1993

that the ice problems can be solved and that they will not give rise to serious environmental damage.
The studies point to serious problems. The only response the federal government could make to the federal environmental assessment panel which recommended against building the bridge was to conclude that these ice problems were manageable. There was not any effective justification for that conclusion.
We should be concerned when the fishermen of Prince Edward Island unanimously oppose the fixed link on the grounds that it will harm their fishery. We heard a great deal today how this fixed link will not harm the fishery. Why then would representatives of the 773 island fishermen resolve at their annual meeting on February 6 to oppose the construction of the bridge until effective environmental assessment has been conducted and the true impact of the bridge could be assessed.
Surely we cannot ignore the views of those who work and live off the fishery in the vicinity of where the link will be built. Why would we want to do that? Why would we want to fly in the face of their advice with regard to the potential problems to the fishery?
In 1990 there was an Environmental Assessment Review Panel. It was the federal government's own panel. It rejected a fixed link for a number of reasons, such as the marine ecosystems and agricultural microclimates arising from the potential for delayed spring ice melting. There is the risk of damage to spawning grounds. We have limited knowledge of the Northumberland Strait ecosystem which makes it difficult to predict the environmental impact of such a link.
The review panel opposed the construction of a link because it was regarded as being incompatible with sustainable development and because inadequate consideration was given to the cumulative impact of building such a link.
The panel also opposed the link because of the difficulties in finding socially acceptable work solutions for displaced ferry workers and fishermen and because of inadequate consideration of the environmental and ecological impact on Prince Edward Island as a result of increased patterns of tourist growth. There were also problems concerning land use issues in Prince Edward Island.
Government Orders
In its conclusion, the panel said there is a need for an improved transportation system between Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, something we all accept. However, after careful consideration the panel concluded that the risk of harmful effects of the proposed bridge concept is unacceptable.
The panel therefore recommended that the project not proceed. Instead of taking notice of that review panel, the federal government basically ignored it, issued a report of its own and said the review panel's concerns about the construction and operation of the bridge were either mistaken, misguided or easily dealt with.
It is a hoax to say we have had effective environmental assessment of the fixed link. It appears to be the case that both the provincial Liberal government and the federal Conservative government are prepared to turn a blind eye to any harmful environmental impacts.
I think it is clear that there are enormous gaps in information, data and understanding of how this region works. It would be totally unacceptable to move ahead without a more effective environmental review of the situation. On the basis of environmental concerns, the fixed link just does not stand up. Prince Edward Islanders deserve better from their provincial Liberal government and their federal Conservative government as well as their Liberal MPs who do not seem to be speaking for ordinary Prince Edward Islanders but for the business community and are not at all interested in the true impacts on Prince Edward Island life and the sea around the link.
I would just like to close by making a few comments about the economics of this fixed link. At the moment Marine Atlantic, which is responsible for the ferry services, is one of the island's largest employers with a wage bill of almost $17 million. Over the 35 years, the time for which the federal government would replace the cost of running the ferries with a subsidy to this private corporation which will be building and running the link, that would constitute some $588 billion lost to Prince Edward Island. That does not include any increases in workers' salaries and wages over that time.
Prince County in Prince Edward Island experiences the highest level of unemployment of all the counties on the island. The loss there as a result of building this link rather than continuing with an improved ferry service, which would be entirely feasible and economical, would be 422 jobs or some $430 million over that period of time.

Government Orders
The economic impact on the region most affected would be catastrophic to say the least.
If the ferry service was improved it would be an economically sustainable method of transportation. If we maintained and expanded it we could address the concerns of Prince Edward Islanders and those who wish to visit there for both commercial and tourist reasons.
A study conducted for the Department of Public Works also makes it clear that the economic viability of this project is a serious problem. In a report by Gardner Pinfold in 1992, the conclusion is made that if economic viability is an important criterion for proceeding with the project, it would be advisable to conduct a more rigorous analysis.
The conclusion of another report by Professor Townley of Acadia University mentioned by my colleague earlier states that the economic assessments which have been done do not establish the economic viability of a fixed crossing.
There are serious economic and environmental questions about the viability of this fixed link. When Prince Edward Islanders were asked whether or not they were in favour of a link between the mainland and Prince Edward Island they were not faced with the question of bridge only, they were faced with a choice between a bridge and a tunnel. They were also asked whether or not more research should be done on the project.
The response from Prince Edward Islanders is ambiguous with regard to their acceptability of the link. If any members care to visit Prince Edward Island they will find many islanders opposed to the link for the reasons I have mentioned, primarily environmental and because they fear that the island's way of life will be destroyed forever.
It is unfortunate that none of the Liberals MPs from Prince Edward Island will speak out on behalf of those who raised serious questions about the impact of this link.
This is an attempt to improve the economic situation of Prince Edward Island and it is to be supported. We cannot go around this country building megaprojects which harm the environment. We cannot continue to
treat the environment as if it does not count or cost anything, as if the implications on it do not have a major impact on our future way of life.
We know that our environment is in serious danger, yet the government and the Liberal Party are prepared to go ahead with this link in spite of those environmental concerns.
It would be foolhardy and environmentally dangerous, and economically it does not make sense.

They drop in to my province for a few hours occasionally during the year and suddenly become experts on the province. They know very well that the labour unions in Prince Edward Island are in favour of the fixed link. I have letters in my office from the labour unions of Prince Edward Island supporting the link.
Officially the fishermen's associations would like to have an environmental assessment but many fishermen in Prince Edward Island support the fixed link. It is okay for the New Democratic Party to stand up and give all the reasons why we cannot have any development there. It is okay to support the St. Lawrence Seaway which ruined our ports in Atlantic Canada many years ago. We continue to support that seaway which goes to Thunder Bay and takes the prairie grain out to the Atlantic. It is okay to support weight subsidy for grain transport to British Columbia ports but it is not okay for Prince Edward Island to have a link to the mainland to facilitate the transport of its products to market.
I find it really incredulous that the NDP continues to harp and harp, in this manner, about a bridge across the Northumberland Strait. It is time to vote on this and take it to second reading so we can review what has been done. We can review the 92 environmental studies that have been done over the past seven years. We can review and question the economics of this proposal.
I am really tired of listening to this type of criticism from the New Democratic Party. We should vote on this and get it to second reading so we can bring in our expert witnesses from all sides. Then we can satisfy ourselves as
