members of Parliament whether or not this is a feasible project.

Mr. Speaker, it is evident that the member has not been listening to much of what has been going on in the House today because it is clear that New Democrats are not opposed to economic development in any region of Canada. Indeed, we fully support efforts to improve the economic situation of Prince Edward Island.
It would be foolhardy to ignore the environmental implications because in the long term that will not benefit Prince Edward Island or Prince Edward Islanders.
It would be foolhardy to support the legislation to implement the fixed link in principle without fully considering its implications. You cannot go ahead and ignore the economic and environmental consequences of such a major project. It makes much more sense to make our assessments first before supporting the issue in principle.
I do not want to suggest to the Liberal members of Parliament from Prince Edward Island how to do their jobs, even though they do not like us to criticize the environmental and adverse economic implications of this link. Surely they should be a little more holistic and concerned about the total impact of something of this magnitude. They should be asking more effective questions about what the impact of this link would be.
The member mentioned the trade unions in Prince Edward Island. He will no doubt be aware of a recent letter written to the newspapers in Prince Edward Island from the president of the Prince Edward Island Federation of Labour where serious questions were raised about the economic and environmental implications of the link. His letter says: "I only hope that the Islanders promoting the bridge are right because a lot of people will be hurt and hurt severely if they are wrong". That hardly seems to constitute support for such a major project.
Let us just stop for a moment and consider the economic and environmental implications. Let us not just go full speed ahead without considering these implications.

Mr. Speaker, I very much appreciate the ability to enter the debate this afternoon. I think it is important for someone from the middle of Canada to take the time to express the relevance of this specific piece of legislation to the House.
I know that this government and this cabinet minister, the Minister of Public Works, are very concerned about public transportation issues. He went to great lengths to resolve a very significant transportation issue within my own constituency.
There is a certain amount of hypocrisy coming from the NDP. When we were trying to resolve this issue in my riding the members opposite criticized the government for not moving quickly enough to resolve a transportation issue. Today the members opposite are criticizing the government for possibly moving too fast.
I would like to move into a little more reserved and detailed presentation. I would like to thank those who took the time to help me do the research on this particular piece of my presentation because it is quite detailed and it is quite important that it be added to the debate.
I first want to address the history of our transportation links to Prince Edward Island and how this incredible project will benefit the people of the island and the Atlantic provinces.
Under the 1873 conditions of union with Prince Edward Island, the government committed to, and I quote: "maintain efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers".
Since the earliest days of Confederation the federal government has placed a high priority on meeting its commitment to the province to provide a transportation link to the island.
I would like to explain how we have met our commitment to the province to link the island with the rest of Canada over the years.
Prior to 1917 the routing of marine service for the carriage of passengers and freight to the island changed with the seasons. Ferry terminals were built at Borden and Cape Tormentime to coincide with the introduction of a new ice-breaking ferry, the SS Prince Edward Island. This ferry entered service in 1917 and provided the first capability to carry rail cars to the island.

February 22, 1993
Government Orders
In 1923 the Canadian National Railway began to operate this service. The SS Charlottetown was introduced in 1923 as a companion to the SS Prince Edward Island. However, in 1941 the SS Charlottetown ran aground and was a total loss.
The first diesel-powered vessel, the MV Abegweit was introduced to the service in 1947 and was capable of carrying both autos and rail cars. The MV Confederation was introduced to service in 1962 and later moved to the Wood Islands-Caribou route.
In 1968 the MV John Hamilton Gray was constructed for the service at a cost of $14 million at which time the SS Prince Edward Island was retired. The mainstays of the Prince Edward Island fleet, the MV Holiday Island and the MV Vacationland, have been serving the island since 1971. These vessels introduced navigational efficiencies to the service because they have a unique navigation propulsion system which has proven to be both efficient and effective. In 1982 the old MV Abegweit was replaced by a new MV Abegweit, a large modem ice-breaker. I understand it was a considerable expense to the government to build that particular ferry.
When Marine Atlantic was incorporated in the mid-1980s it was entrusted with the responsibility to operate and maintain the Borden-Cape Tormentine ferry service on behalf of the federal government. While it is financially dependent on the federal government, over recent years Marine Atlantic has made some improvements to the level of cost recovery for its ferry operations, to the extent possible, given the economic realities of Atlantic Canada. This has been achieved by reducing costs and increasing revenue levels wherever possible.
It must be kept in mind though that the cost of capital acquisitions for the ferry service is high. A recent estimate of the cost to replace one of the vessels in the Prince Edward Island fleet puts the capital costs of the vessel at $95 million. I think some of my colleagues have mentioned the high cost of investment earlier in the debate; in fact, there was one commentary where one of the most recent vessels added to the fleet cost in excess of $200 million. It is a very expensive venture.
The federal government has also provided financial assistance for the ferry service operating between Wood Islands, Prince Edward Island and Caribou, Nova Scotia. This has been operating since 1938. The operation of this service has been provided by the Northumberland Ferries Ltd. since 1941.
The House may recall that the government is investing over $60 million for the construction of a new ship for the Wood Islands run. This includes the construction of the terminals necessary and all the infrastructure to get this initiative up and running. This initiative has resulted in the creation of jobs in Pictou and Caribou, Nova Scotia and Wood Islands, Prince Edward Island, in addition to providing an important addition to the ferry transportation link between the island and Nova Scotia.
It is the view of the government that the transportation sector is part of the basic infrastructure of Canada. Transportation is essential to the daily economic and social life of this great nation by joining the many regions and moving goods and people from coast to coast. The construction of a bridge to span the nine miles from Borden, Prince Edward Island to Cape Tormentine on the mainland is one of the largest private sector engineering challenges ever to be undertaken in this country.
I come from Manitoba where hydroelectridty is a very significant part of our infrastructure and I know what the results are of these significant projects on the provincial economy. The fact that a new hydro development project in Manitoba is up and running has a significant impact on all the communities throughout Manitoba, and I would expect that this construction project will have a very significant impact on the economies of all the Atlantic provinces.
I am pleased to acknowledge the hard work of my colleague, the Minister of Public Works, in bringing this important project to its present stage. He has met the challenges of a complex public environmental review process and he has studied and complied with stringent environmental criteria related to the bridge design.
The unique approach to this project whereby the bridge will be financed, constructed, owned, operated and maintained by the private sector has been developed in an effort to minimize the cost to government. While the developer will assume all normal construction,
February 22, 1993

operation and maintenance risks, in return it will receive an annual government subsidy for a period of 35 years.
It is important to note that paying a subsidy for 35 years will result in a bridge that for the remaining 65 years of its expected design life will require no government subsidy assistance at all. This represents a significant future saving to Canadian taxpayers. In addition the operation and maintenance of the bridge will be funded on a user-pay basis through the collection of tolls.
We have debated a number of times over the last while in the House on the user-pay theory that has been put forward by this government. This is just another prime example where user pay is the appropriate way to go and is in support of any one of a number of government functions.
It is important to note that an estimated 3,500 person-years of employment will be created in the Atlantic region over the five-year construction period directly related to the bridge project. We can also talk about the fact that there are significant spin-offs outside the bridge project itself.
We cannot and do not ignore the fact that there will also be an enormous impact on the present Marine Atlantic ferry workers. We hope it will be found that an acceptable compensation and adjustment package will be in place to assist these employees who have contributed so much to their communities.
Nonetheless we are undertaking this project because we firmly believe that this bridge will have an enormous effect on modernizing transportation access to the island. We certainly anticipate with optimism that the dramatic improvement in accessibility to the island will have a very positive impact on Prince Edward Island's tourism industry.
A modem Canadian transport system is important to Canadian consumers and to our industrial sectors. Efficient transportation access is directly related to the competitiveness of Canadian goods and services on markets at home and abroad. For these reasons the federal government has always been and will continue to be committed to the future of the transportation industry in Canada.
In closing, it is my hope that all members of the House will join me in supporting Bill C-110 so that we may proceed with this important and historic national under-

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to enter into the debate on the fixed link project.
The $900 million bridge proposed by Strait Crossing would replace federally subsidized ferry service between the two provinces. The government is willing to provide the developer with an annual subsidy over the next 35 years which would otherwise go to the ferry. The subsidy would then disappear with the government assuming ownership of the bridge which has a design life of 100 years.
This sizeable project of $900 million has not undergone the proper environmental studies, the proper socioeconomic studies. The ferry workers are also stating that they are unhappy with the lack of information coming from the premier's office on a compensation package should they lose their jobs to the link. They want answers and they want them soon. These are the kinds of things to be done before and not after a project is undertaken.
I come from British Columbia where there are many of these big megaprojects. I was the mayor of the city of Revelstoke when the big hydroelectric dams went in there. We had virtually three years of studies on the socioeconomic impact and how it affects communities. Where will the gravel come from for the massive amount of cement that is going to be used? What kind of environmental effects is that going to have on those parts of the country? What kinds of effects is it going to have on the communities close by? What will be the social impact on those communities? None of these questions have been answered.
In November the finance minister came in with a megaproject just before an election, a $900 million project for P.E.I., a link from P.E.I. to the mainland. He came in with this massive project. One of the main contractors is based in Calgary. Someone comments about the political impact of those four members of Parliament.
I would ask the political question: What about the donations to the federal parties? What about political donations to the governing party? A project of this magnitude is interesting. We will not find that out until the election is over and we look at the Election Expenses

Act to find out who contributed to the Conservative Party and who brought forward these kinds of funds. There is a long list of items.
I also want to talk about what happens when projects of this size come on stream, how they affect the communities, how they affect the hospitals that are needed, how they affect the services, the ambulance services and various other services that are required.
A community needs some time to know where the gravel is coming from, where the social base is coming from, where the education is coming from, and where the structure is going to be set in place to bring this about. Evidently the Liberals and the Conservatives have no concern about that. The main thing is to get the project on stream.
There is a ferry service in place that is handling that service, that transportation. There is no need for rushing on the part of the government to push through a project like this one. There is a need for people to go to work and the social impacts of that. We have called for infrastructure programs with municipalities. We have called for training of employees to get workers back. Why is the government not looking at these kinds of programs rather than this hare-brained idea of a fixed link to the mainland? If the government were to look at these kinds of projects, I would give it one.
There is a piece of highway from Banff National Park to Golden, British Columbia. It can only be described as a cow trail. I have been in contact with the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Finance stating that the highway should be upgraded. We have a four-lane highway from Calgary to Banff. It goes down to a two-lane highway and then hits Field, British Columbia, and can only be described as a cow trail.
There is a court case going on in Golden right now, or in the Kootenays, with regard to serious accidents that have taken place on that piece of highway which was never built to number one TransCanada Highway standards. There is 18 per cent unemployment in the Kootenays. Here is a project the government could have gone into if it wanted to bring about programs to upgrade our transportation systems and meet the needs of the future.
I do not want to say to P.E.I. that it should not have its projects or that it should not have its methods. However, surely to goodness when we have the debt structure this government is talking about there are ways to upgrade ferry services such as we have done in British Columbia, to bring that about and to look at the other programs available to us.
Infrastructure in Canada, our sewer systems, our water systems and various other systems in our municipalities, can only be described as deplorable in many areas. The municipalities want to go, in many cases the provinces want to go, and the federal government says no, that it will not participate in those kinds of programs.
We do have a problem. We have a government that is trying just before an election to come out with some megaprojects, not only to create one of its dreams in the Atlantic provinces but to provide some funding for its next election campaign from big contractors who bid on these projects and donate to the government of the day. It uses those kinds of projects to get itself re-elected. It is in a kind of dream world with regard to these types of projects.
The project will not bring about the fiscal responsibilities that should be in a transportation act. It will not provide the kind of employment that is needed across Canada. It will not provide competitiveness. Some members over there like to use the word competitiveness: "We need some competitiveness in this government to be able to be competitive in the world market". Where is it going to bring about the competitiveness? While this link is being built, Canadian Pacific Railway is talking about tearing up its tracks.
Here is the government using government money to subsidize a bridge while the railways are saying they are going to tear up the tracks. The railways should be paying for that bridge, if that is what they are going to do. If they are going to tear up that track, with all of the lands and all of the assets they were given, the railways should be the ones that are providing the fixed link so that the transportation can come by truck, if that is what the railways are deciding.
